earnings.headline: Centuri had a record quarter: sales grew 40% and it kept more profit from each sales dollar, though a couple of units slipped.
points: Sales (revenue) hit a record $1.2 billion, up 40% from a year ago. All four business units grew.
Net income (profit after all costs) was $26.9 million, up from $2.1 million in the same quarter last year.
Profit kept per sales dollar (gross margin) rose to 9.5% from 9.2%, but Canada's fell to 19.6% from 21.9%.
Their own forecast (guidance) for 2026 sales is $3.8 to $3.9 billion. It assumes no storm repair work in the fourth quarter.
They build, fix and upgrade gas and power lines for utility companies across the U.S. and Canada, mostly under long-term contracts.
Their top 20 customers made up 65% of sales in fiscal 2025, so a lot depends on a few big utilities.
Former parent Southwest Gas Holdings sold all of its shares in 2025, so Centuri now runs fully on its own.
Risks they name: weather, cost overruns on fixed-price jobs, rising costs, labor shortages, and lawsuits like a City of Chicago case.
Insider trades: director Carl Icahn sold $33.7M of stock, while directors Patton and Mariucci bought shares.
Other headlines cover the Q3 earnings call and results that came in ahead of what analysts expected.

takeaways: The business grew fast this quarter, with record sales and more profit kept from each dollar of sales.
Debt is lighter compared to earnings: 2.6x now vs 3.8x a year ago. Lower means less strain from borrowing.
Forecasts are not promises. Storm work, costs and a few big customers can swing results either way.

earnings.headline: Carvana sold a record number of cars and made more total profit, but it earned less on each car than a year ago.
points: Sold 217,385 cars, up 39% from a year ago, while the overall car market stayed about flat.
Revenue (sales) was $8.040 billion, up 42%. Net income (profit after all costs) was $483 million.
Profit per car fell to $6,997, down $365. Higher fuel costs and rising interest rates cut about $200 per car.
Their own forecast (guidance): more cars sold next quarter, and Adjusted EBITDA (a profit measure) near the top of $2.7 to $3.0 billion.
They make money selling used cars online, giving car loans to buyers, and selling cars that miss their standards at wholesale.
Since 2012 they have sold 2.8 million cars and brought in $84.1 billion in total sales.
Big risks they name: heavy debt, needing to raise more money, and relying on selling car loans for much of their profit.
Other risks: a recession hurting car buying, high interest rates, and the Garcia family controlling the company.
An investor lawsuit claims Carvana misled people about title and registration (the paperwork to legally own a car).
Several articles debate whether the stock is priced too high and what weaker used-car demand could do to the business.
One research firm, Stifel, started covering the company with a positive view of its growth in cars sold.

takeaways: Carvana is growing fast and making more total profit, but it earns a bit less on each car than last year.
Starting with their next earnings call, they plan to stop giving quarterly or yearly forecasts and focus on long-term goals.
The company carries a lot of debt and faces an investor lawsuit about car paperwork. Both are real risks to keep in mind.

earnings.headline: Sales grew 40% and the company raised its forecast again, but it still lost money, mostly because of a one-time cost tied to its debt.
points: Sales (revenue) were $321 million, up 40% from a year ago. It was the fifth quarter in a row that growth sped up.
They lost $43 million overall. The main cause was a one-time $57 million cost of buying back some of their debt early.
Operating income (profit from day-to-day business) fell 27% to $33 million. Not every profit measure got better.
Their own forecast (guidance): Q4 sales of $348 to $351 million, up 44% to 45%, and 60%+ sales growth in 2027.
They rent out computing power over the internet (a "cloud"), including AI chips, mainly to growing tech companies.
They focus on smaller firms. A research firm expects that market to grow from $138 billion in 2025 to $251 billion in 2028.
They are pushing hard into AI, including tools for "agents" (AI programs that do tasks on their own).
Risks they name: results can swing a lot, profits may not last, and growth could slow as the business gets bigger.
Several headlines say the stock went up, including an 11% gain on a day when tech shares bounced back.
One investment fund opened a new $98.1M position in the stock.
Some articles give outside opinions on what the stock is worth. Those are guesses, not company facts.

takeaways: Sales are growing fast, up 40%, mostly from AI customers. The company's own forecast says growth will speed up even more.
On paper they lost money this quarter. Most of that loss came from a one-time cost of paying down debt.
Big customers (over $100,000 a year) now bring in 41% of sales. Growth depends on AI demand and on building data centers in time.

earnings.headline: Dover's sales and profit both grew in the third quarter, and it still expects double-digit adjusted profit growth per share for 2026.
points: Sales (revenue) were $2.2 billion, up 8% from a year ago. Not counting newly bought businesses, sales still grew 7%.
Profit per share was $2.50, up 14%. The adjusted version, which leaves out one-time items, was $2.88, up 10%.
Guidance (their own forecast) for 2026: profit per share of $8.93 to $9.08 and sales growth of 7% to 8%.
Orders rose in all five units and beat shipments. On the downside, restructuring costs and losses from sold businesses grew.
Dover makes equipment, parts and software in five units, from fueling gear and refrigeration to marking printers and pumps.
About 46% of sales come from outside the United States, which exposes Dover to tariffs, trade limits and political trouble abroad.
It sold its Environmental Solutions Group in 2024 for $2.0 billion, so those results are now counted separately.
Named risks: recessions, rising labor costs or strikes, worker shortages, and employee misconduct that could bring fines.
Most headlines are stock forecasts and price targets from finance sites, not news about the business itself.
Dover presented at an industrial conference, and one site says refinancing its debt could be a notable update.
Two board members each received 970 stock units, paid out as shares when their board service ends.

takeaways: Dover is growing: sales and profit both rose this quarter and so far this year.
Orders are stacking up, with much of the backlog (orders not yet shipped) set to ship in 2027.
It's not all smooth: restructuring costs rose, and tariffs, recessions and labor costs are real risks.

earnings.headline: Dow's sales and profit rose a lot from a weak year ago, mainly because prices went up, though it sold slightly less.
points: Sales were $11.3 billion, up 13% from a year ago, mostly because prices rose 14%. Volume (amount sold) fell 1%.
Profit (net income) was $525 million, up from $124 million. Earnings per share were $0.62, up from $0.08.
Bad spot: the Middle East conflict hurt sales in Asia Pacific, and one segment sold 7% less than a year ago.
Their own forecast: cost cuts and plant closures should add more than $1 billion of profit (EBITDA) in both 2026 and 2027.
Dow makes plastics and chemicals for packaging, buildings, cars and home goods. Sales were $40 billion in 2025.
2025 was rough: sales fell 7 percent and Dow lost $3.70 per share, after earning $1.57 per share in 2024.
They booked $1,856 million in charges for restructuring and write-downs, and cut about 1,500 jobs to save money.
Risks they name: asbestos lawsuits (7,158 claims open at end of 2025), wars, energy and raw material prices.
One headline says Dow's shares are up 41% so far this year.
Other articles weigh what analysts think of the stock; several headlines are about the Dow Jones index, not this company.

takeaways: Higher prices for their plastics lifted sales and profit sharply compared with a weak quarter a year ago.
They are selling slightly less, and the Middle East conflict is a real drag on parts of the business.
2025 was a loss year. This quarter shows recovery, but energy costs, raw materials and lawsuits remain risks.

earnings.headline: Domino's grew sales and profit this quarter, but sales at existing stores were nearly flat and cash left over fell.
points: Sales (revenue) rose 3.4% to $1,185.6 million, mostly from more food sold to stores and more franchise fees.
Profit (net income) rose 9.2% to $152.2 million. Profit per share was $4.60, up from $4.08 a year ago.
Sales at older U.S. stores barely grew, up 0.3% vs 5.2% a year ago. Older stores abroad were up just 0.2%.
Free cash flow (cash left after costs) fell 7.2% to $459.8 million so far this year, partly from the timing of ad payments.
About 99% of stores are run by franchise owners. Domino's earns fees (royalties) on their sales and sells them food.
It has more than 22,100 locations in over 90 markets and calls itself the largest pizza company in the world.
Its U.S. pizza market share rose to about 23.3% in 2025, up from about 22.5% the year before.
Biggest named risks: heavy debt, cheese and other food costs, labor, rivals and delivery apps, and weaker spending.
Analyst firm Baird raised its view, saying it sees a clearer path to better sales and franchisee profits.
Headlines note the stock is up 11.1% since the last earnings report.
A company officer plans to sell 370 shares received as part of their pay.

takeaways: Domino's is still growing, but slowly: more stores and more profit, while sales at existing stores were almost flat.
Profit grew faster than sales, helped by cheaper food buying and the company buying back its own shares.
The weak spots: cash coming in dropped this year, the company carries a lot of debt, and it gave no number forecast.

earnings.headline: Sales rose 5.1% to $3.2 billion, but profit per share fell to $2.05 from $2.19 a year ago.
points: Sales (money coming in) rose 5.1% to $3.2 billion. LongHorn Steakhouse led, with same-restaurant sales up 6.2%.
Profit per share was $2.05, down from $2.19. Last year included a one-time gain from selling Olive Garden Canada.
Leaving out one-time items, profit per share rose 4.1% from last year's $1.97. Olive Garden sales grew only 1.1%.
Their own forecast (guidance) is unchanged: $11.10 to $11.35 profit per share for the full year.
They make money running sit-down restaurants like Olive Garden and LongHorn: 2,202 owned in the US as of May 31, 2026.
Another 167 restaurants are run by other companies under franchise deals, using Darden's brand names.
This year they sold eight Olive Garden restaurants in Canada and started weighing options for Bahama Breeze.
Biggest risks they name: rising food, wage and energy costs, tariffs, and guests eating out less when money is tight.
Headlines say the stock hit an all-time high, and several track what Wall Street analysts think of it.
Darden plans to share its next results on Dec. 18 in a call with a webcast and Q&A.
Some stories cover higher dividends (cash paid to owners); the latest declared is $1.62 per share.

takeaways: More people are spending at Darden: sales grew and every group of brands had higher same-restaurant sales.
Profit per share was lower than a year ago on paper, mostly because last year had a one-time sale gain.
Costs rose too, and short-term debt grew to $979.7 million from $693.6 million, so that is worth watching.

earnings.headline: Sales were $3.578 billion, but profit fell from last quarter and cash flow fell from a year ago, while the low end of the forecast rose.
points: Sales (revenue) were $3.578 billion. Each treatment brought in $415.25, a bit less than $415.87 last quarter.
Profit fell to $3.40 per share from $4.02 last quarter, partly from a $62 million write-down (lower value) of its China unit.
Cash left after running costs (free cash flow) was $276 million, down from $604 million a year ago.
Their own forecast (guidance) for adjusted profit per share is now $14.30 to $15.20. The low end used to be $14.10.
DaVita makes most of its money running dialysis centers. Dialysis is a treatment that cleans the blood when kidneys fail.
It also runs care programs that try to slow kidney disease and lower total health costs. It has centers outside the U.S. too.
Biggest risk it names: profits lean on patients with private insurance, who pay more, and those payment rates keep getting squeezed.
Other named risks: Medicare payment cuts, rising worker pay, supply problems, its debt, and a 2025 cyberattack.
One headline says the company expects fewer dialysis treatments, which is seen as a possible weak spot.
DaVita says it now offers an advanced dialysis therapy at every U.S. center.
Several articles focus on how much cash the company makes and what analysts think of it.

takeaways: Sales held steady, but profit per share and cash flow came in lower than in the periods they were compared to.
This quarter, the cost of each treatment went up while the money earned per treatment dipped a little.
The company slightly raised the bottom of its own yearly forecast and keeps buying back its own shares.

earnings.headline: Devon made strong cash, cut debt and raised its merger savings goal, but a few areas came in weaker than planned.
points: Sales of oil, gas and NGL (natural gas liquids) were $5.9 billion. Profit was $1.0 billion, or $0.88 per share.
Cash from operations was $2.8 billion. After paying for drilling, $2.0 billion was left over (free cash flow).
Their own forecast (guidance) for 2026 is unchanged. For 2027, after a sale, they expect about 525,000 barrels of oil per day.
Weak spots: Eagle Ford oil came in below plan, and field running costs were slightly above their own forecast range.
Devon makes money by pumping and selling oil, natural gas and NGL (natural gas liquids), mostly in the U.S.
At the end of 2025, debt was $8.4 billion. $7.4 billion of it had fixed interest rates averaging 5.7%.
Big change: on February 1, 2026 Devon agreed to merge with Coterra. A named risk is not getting the hoped-for benefits.
Other named risks: swings in oil and gas prices, tariffs, pipeline limits, government and climate rules, and its debt.
Headlines cover the $8 billion buyback (the company buying its own shares) and the $4.2 billion asset sale.
Analysts disagree: JPMorgan raised its price target, while Raymond James cut its target on weaker oil prices.
One headline says the stock fell 19% over 5 straight down days. Activist shareholders want Devon to sell itself.

takeaways: Devon is making a lot of cash and using it to pay dividends ($0.32 a share), buy back shares and pay down debt.
It still owes $10.6 billion. It aims to get down to $9 billion in early 2027 using cash and the Eagle Ford sale money.
Results depend heavily on oil and gas prices, and the merger savings and the Eagle Ford sale still have to happen.

earnings.headline: Sales grew 11% and core profit improved, so Dexcom raised its own forecast for the year, though final profit dipped slightly.
points: Sales (revenue) grew 11% to $1.344 billion. U.S. sales grew 14%, but sales outside the U.S. grew only 5%.
Operating profit (profit from the core business) rose to $327.2 million, from $242.5 million a year ago.
Net income (final profit) dipped to $275.1 million from $283.8 million, because last year had more one-off other income.
They raised their full-year sales forecast (guidance) to $5.20 - $5.25 billion and OK'd up to $1.0 billion in share buybacks.
Dexcom makes money selling glucose sensors that help people with diabetes track their blood sugar, like Dexcom G7 and Stelo.
Risk they name: if prices for their products fall and they can't cut costs, profits could suffer.
Risk they name: insurers don't always cover their sensors, and getting paid can be a hassle, which could hurt sales.
Risk they name: they must answer an FDA (U.S. health regulator) warning letter, and making enough product could be a problem.
Some headlines ask whether a Medicare delay is the biggest risk for the company.
Dexcom marked the opening of its Athenry plant with a commercial production milestone.
Most other headlines are opinion pieces and forecasts about the stock, not news about the business itself.

takeaways: Sales and core profits are growing, and the company raised its own forecast for the year.
Final profit slipped a bit versus last year, and sales outside the U.S. are growing more slowly.
The risks they name are real: insurance coverage, falling prices, an FDA warning letter, and making enough product.

earnings.headline: Clean Harbors had a record quarter: sales rose 21% to $1.87 billion, profit jumped 75%, and it raised its own forecast for 2026.
points: Sales (revenue) rose 21% to a record $1.87 billion, up from $1.55 billion a year earlier. Both main businesses grew.
Profit (net income) rose 75% to $208.1 million, or $3.93 per share, compared with $118.8 million a year ago.
Guidance (their own forecast) went up. They now expect 2026 Adjusted EBITDA, a core profit measure, of $1.44 billion to $1.48 billion.
Caution: one big emergency cleanup brought in about $120 million. Jobs like that don't come every quarter. Refinery work stayed soft.
They collect, treat, recycle and dispose of hazardous waste at over 100 sites. They also turn used oil into new oil products.
In 2025, sales rose 2.4% to $6,030.8 million, but profit fell 2.8% to $391.0 million.
Sales at the used-oil unit fell $47.4 million in 2025. Prices for its oil products dropped and it sold less.
Biggest risks they name: accidents and spills at dangerous sites, tech failures or cyber attacks, and cheaper new ways to handle waste.
Investigators say an explosion at a Clean Harbors hazardous waste plant came after two earlier fires there.
Several articles debate whether the stock price is too high after the strong results and the CEO change.
A company director, Marcy L. Reed, gave away 350 shares as a gift, according to a required filing.

takeaways: Business was very strong this quarter: more sales, much more profit, and a higher forecast for the year.
Part of the jump came from one big emergency job and high oil prices. Those may not last.
Leadership is changing: Eric Gerstenberg becomes sole CEO on January 1. A plant explosion is also under investigation.

earnings.headline: Sales slipped and a $1,050.0 million write-down caused a big loss, but adjusted profit and cash flow held up and the dividend rose.
points: Sales (revenue) were $2,453.7 million, down (1.2)% from $2,483.3 million a year earlier.
A non-cash write-down of $1,050.0 million (an asset now valued lower) led to an operating loss of $(910.3) million.
Without that charge and other one-offs, operating profit edged up to $309.0 million from $305.1 million.
Their own forecast (guidance) for next quarter: sales of $2.410 billion to $2.460 billion, a (5.0)% to (3.0)% drop excluding currency.
They run customer service, sales and back-office work for more than 2,000 clients, paid mostly by staff hours or tasks handled.
About 455,000 staff work in 74 countries; about 89% of sales came from outside the U.S. in 2025, up from 88% in 2024.
Risks they name: cyberattacks, high staff turnover, currency swings and tariffs.
Clients can end contracts early for any reason, usually with 30 to 90 days' notice.
A law firm, Pomerantz, says it is investigating claims on behalf of Concentrix investors.
Several stories cover the company's launch of an AI migration tool.
Filings show large funds, including AQR, holding stakes in the company.

takeaways: Sales are shrinking a little, and the company expects more shrinking next quarter as AI changes its old business.
The huge loss was mostly an accounting write-down tied to a lower stock price, not cash out the door, but it is still bad news.
Cash keeps coming in ($268.2 million this quarter) and the dividend rose to $0.37, while a law firm is looking into investor claims.

earnings.headline: Crocs grew sales 4.6% to $1,043 million and raised its own full-year forecast for the third time this year.
points: Sales rose 4.6% to $1,043 million. The Crocs brand grew 4.4%, and HEYDUDE grew 6.1% after a weak 2025.
Profit per share was $4.52, up from $2.70. Without one-time items it was $3.69, up from $2.92: still solid, but smaller.
Their own forecast (guidance) for 2026 sales is now up about 3%, raised from up 1% to 2% before.
Weak spot: Crocs brand sales in North America fell 2.1%. The growth came from overseas, where sales rose 11.8%.
They sell Crocs and HEYDUDE shoes to other stores (wholesale) and straight to shoppers online and in their own shops.
In 2025, sales fell 1.5%. HEYDUDE sales dropped 13.3%, while the Crocs brand grew 1.5%.
They cut HEYDUDE's value on the books by $430.0 million (brand name) and $307.0 million (goodwill), so 2025 ended in a loss.
Risks they name: extra import taxes (duties) cut gross margin by 130 basis points, plus currency swings and limits from their debt.
Headlines say overseas sales rose 12% and ask whether that growth can last.
Several stories note the stock hit a new 52-week high after the earnings report.
A Crocs x Barkbox dog bed that sold out in minutes is back in stock.

takeaways: The business got better this year: sales and profit are up, and HEYDUDE is growing again after a rough 2025.
Part of the profit jump comes from one-time items like tariff refunds, so the adjusted numbers give a truer picture.
Growth now leans on buyers outside the US, where Crocs shoe sales slipped. Debt is still about $1.29 billion.

earnings.headline: Centene posted a small loss by official accounting rules, but its core business earned more and it raised its 2026 forecast.
points: Sales (revenue) rose 0.5% to $45.1 billion. Fewer Marketplace and Medicaid members held growth back.
Official result: a loss of $(0.14) per share. Leaving out one-time costs like layoffs, profit was $0.58 per share.
They raised their own 2026 forecast (guidance): adjusted profit over $5.20 a share, up $0.40 from before.
Marketplace members fell to 3,403,300 from 5,828,100 a year ago. The quarter used $3.7 billion of cash.
They run government-backed health plans: Medicaid (low-income people), Medicare (seniors) and Marketplace plans.
In 2025, total sales were $194.8 billion. Medicaid brought in 57% of sales from outside customers.
In 2025, medical costs rose faster than expected, from more care use and pricey new drugs.
Biggest risks they name: costs beating their price estimates, and a new law that could cut Medicaid members and money.
Headlines say a delay in Medicaid work rules lifted Centene and Molina shares.
Some analysts say the profit repair is real; one says the share price may already reflect it.

takeaways: The core business is earning more, but official results still show a small loss this quarter.
Millions fewer people use their Marketplace plans than a year ago, so sales from that side shrank.
They cut debt by $1.1 billion since June, but Medicaid rule changes remain a big unknown.

earnings.headline: Duolingo says daily users grew faster this quarter and its key money numbers beat its own expectations.
points: Daily users (people who open the app each day) grew 29% from a year ago, and that growth sped up.
The CEO says all key financial numbers came in ahead of expectations. This release gives no sales or profit figures.
Next: keep the free app fun, while slowly pushing harder on bookings (money customers commit to pay).
They say they won't hurt the free version to make more money. Long-term goal: one billion learners.
Money comes from paid plans (Super Duolingo, Duolingo Max), ads for free users, in-app extras, and the Duolingo English Test.
Paid subscribers reached 12.2 million at the end of 2025, up from 9.5 million a year earlier.
2025 profit got a one-time tax boost of $256.7 million, so it looks bigger than normal business alone would show.
Biggest risk they name: losing users, or users using the app less or not paying, which could hurt sales.
Several law firms are promoting a shareholder class-action lawsuit; one lists a deadline of December 7, 2026.
Chief engineering officer Natalie Glance sold $784,742 in company shares.
One headline says the company raised its guidance (its own forecast) as daily user growth sped up.

takeaways: More people are using Duolingo every day, and that growth got faster this quarter.
Paying customers grew a lot in 2025, but a one-time tax benefit made that year's profit look bigger.
A shareholder lawsuit is in the news. These sources don't explain what it claims, so it's an open question.

earnings.headline: Sales and goods sold on eBay grew fast this quarter, but official profit and profit margins fell versus last year.
points: Sales (revenue) were $3.2 billion, up 14% from a year ago. Total value of goods sold (GMV) was $23.2 billion, up 15%.
Official (GAAP) profit fell 16% to $501 million, from $593 million. Profit margin slipped to 19.2% from 20.3%.
Their own forecast (guidance) for Q4 sales is $3.19 - $3.24 billion, growth of 7% - 9%, slower than this quarter's 13%.
They paid $1.4 billion cash for Depop, a used-fashion app, after first agreeing on about $1.2 billion.
eBay makes money mainly from fees on each sale, ads sellers pay for to promote listings, and shipping services.
In 2025, sales rose 8% to $11.1 billion. Ad sales grew 22%. Goods sold on eBay reached nearly $80 billion.
Profit margin fell to 20.5% from 22.5%, due to legal, restructuring and higher shipping costs.
Risks they name: tariffs, the end of a U.S. duty-free rule for small imports, more canceled orders, and weak shopper confidence.
Several headlines discuss eBay's stock rising and whether its share price is fair after the gains.
A company officer sold US$5.12 Million in stock, while one fund opened a new $495.4M position.
eBay also released a 2026 report on collecting trends.

takeaways: eBay is growing: more people are buying and selling used, collectible and pre-loved items there.
Growth has a cost: official profit and profit margins were lower than a year ago.
eBay itself expects slower sales growth next quarter, and it names tariffs and trade rules as real risks.

earnings.headline: Sales grew 13% and adjusted profit per share rose 5%, but reported profit fell as deal and loan costs rose.
points: Sales (money from customers) were $4,694.8 million, up 13%. Organic sales, which leave out newly bought companies, grew 7%.
Reported profit fell 6% to $551.3 million. Deal costs and $70 million more in interest on loans to buy companies weighed on it.
Guidance (their own forecast): adjusted profit per share of $8.10 to $8.20 for 2026, up 8% to 9%.
High-Tech sales, serving chip makers and AI data centers, grew 63%. Pest Elimination's profit margin slipped to 20.3% from 20.9%.
Ecolab sells water, cleaning and infection-prevention products and services. It has $16 billion in yearly sales in 170+ countries.
In 2025, sales grew 2% to $16.1 billion. Adjusted profit per share rose 13% to $7.53. Reported profit per share fell 1% to $7.28.
In December 2025 it paid $1.6 billion in cash for Ovivo Electronics, which makes ultrapure water systems for computer chip factories.
It raised its quarterly dividend (cash paid to owners) 12% to $0.73 per share, its 34th yearly raise in a row.
Wells Fargo analysts raised their view of Ecolab, pointing to AI data center cooling from the CoolIT and Ovivo deals.
Ecolab launched a combined cooling platform aimed at AI data centers.
Morgan Stanley says AI may make Ecolab's moat (its edge over competitors) stronger.

takeaways: The main businesses are growing again, and the chip and AI data center work is growing fastest.
Buying companies costs money now: more interest and deal costs pushed reported profit down this quarter.
Rising raw material costs and trouble in the Middle East are real risks. Higher prices have covered them so far.

earnings.headline: Con Edison earned more this quarter than a year ago, mostly because regulators approved higher electric rates.
points: Profit was $766 million, or $2.07 a share, up from $688 million, or $1.91 a share, a year earlier.
Higher electric rate base (the equipment they may earn on) added $62 million; issuing new shares cut $0.05 a share.
Their own 2026 forecast (guidance) is now $6.05 to $6.15 a share, narrowed from $6.00 to $6.20. Not raised, just tightened.
Nine-month profit got a one-time $134 million boost from selling their stake in a gas pipeline (MVP).
They make money delivering electricity, gas and steam around New York City. Regulators set the prices they can charge.
They serve about 3.7 million electric and 1.1 million gas customers, plus the largest steam system in the U.S.
Big risks they name: strict regulators who can fine them or cap prices, extreme weather, cyber attacks, rising costs.
Customers paying bills slowly has hurt their cash on hand, and they expect that to continue. They are also reviewing their Honeoye stake.
Con Edison launched a 6M-share stock sale. More shares can spread profit thinner per share (called dilution).
Analysts said the quarter beat estimates, and Morningstar wrote that the steady growth plan is on track.
One article says the company's 52-year dividend streak (cash paid to owners) faces 3 major tests.

takeaways: Profit went up compared with last year, mainly from higher rates regulators approved. That money comes from customer bills.
The company kept its full-year forecast in the same middle range. It did not raise it.
They plan about $797 million for weather protection from 2026 through 2030, and are selling new shares to help pay for growth.

earnings.headline: Sales rose and the loss shrank a little, cash grew, but Editas is still losing money and has no product on the market yet.
points: Sales (mostly partner payments) rose to $10.4 million, from $7.5 million a year ago, helped by a partner hitting milestones.
Still losing money: net loss was $23.4 million, a bit smaller than $25.1 million a year ago. Costs rose for research and legal fees.
Cash and investments: $190.2 million, up from $146.6 million. They say it lasts into the second half of 2028.
Next: first patient dosing this year; first safety data expected in the first quarter of 2027. Plans can slip.
No products to sell yet. Money comes from partners (Bristol Myers Squibb, Vertex), patent licensing, and selling new shares.
Main focus: EDIT-401, a one-time gene-editing treatment meant to lower 'bad' LDL cholesterol, moving toward human trials.
Net loss was $160.1 million in 2025; total losses since founding reached $1.6 billion. They say they may never turn a profit.
Biggest risks they name: needing much more funding, and tests or trials that may fail or be delayed.
Insider filings show CEO Gilmore O'Neill sold 21,164 shares.
Executive Linda Burkly acquired 16,533 shares after a research milestone.

takeaways: Editas has no product on the market; it runs on partner payments and cash in the bank while it tests its first medicine.
Loss per share fell to $0.15 from $0.28, partly because there are many more shares now (153,604,267 vs 90,090,397).
The real test is in people: early safety results are expected in the first quarter of 2027. Monkey results may not carry over.

earnings.headline: Sales grew 10% and profit rose, but a weaker U.S. mortgage market made Equifax lower its sales forecast for the year.
points: Sales (revenue) were $1.693 billion for the quarter, up 10% from a year ago.
Profit (net income) was $211.7 million, up 32 percent. Profit per share was $1.79, up from $1.29.
They cut their full-year sales forecast (guidance) to $6.661 billion at the midpoint, because home-loan activity weakened.
Not everything grew: Employer Services sales fell 5 percent, and mortgage sales in Workforce Solutions were about flat.
Equifax sells credit reports, credit scores, fraud checks, and job and income checks to lenders, employers and governments.
About 77% of its sales came from the U.S. in 2025. Home-loan demand changes directly hit its sales and profit.
In 2025 it bought back shares for $927.4 million and raised its quarterly dividend (cash paid to owners) to $0.50 per share.
Biggest risks they name: hackers and data breaches (a past breach hurt sales), and stricter privacy and AI laws.
Recent headlines are mostly analysts sharing opinions on the stock. These are views, not facts or promises.
Some coverage focuses on the mortgage outlook, since home loans are a big driver of Equifax sales.
One article flags debt (leverage) and a high price compared to earnings (valuation) as things to watch.

takeaways: Most of the business grew this quarter, even while the home-loan market got worse.
The company lowered its own forecast for the year because it expects the weak mortgage market to continue.
Equifax holds sensitive personal data, so a security breach is a real risk it has faced before.

earnings.headline: Everest's profit fell as it set aside more money for old claims and paid for disasters, while its investment earnings rose.
points: Sales (premiums from its main businesses) were $3.7 billion, down 4.0% from a year ago.
Profit was $233 million vs $255 million a year ago; investment earnings rose to $634 million from $540 million.
Insurance itself lost money: about $268 million added for old claims, plus disaster losses like the Colombia Earthquake.
No forecast (guidance) given. They bought back $474 million of their own shares and call buybacks a top priority.
Everest sells reinsurance (insurance for insurance companies) and insurance; 2025 premiums were $17.7 billion.
About 72.4% of 2025 premiums came from reinsurance. It sold some retail insurance business to AIG for $252 million.
2025 profit was $1.6 billion, after adding $657 million for older claims that came in worse than expected.
Biggest risks they name: big disasters, climate change, and lawsuit costs pushing claims above their estimates.
Several law firms announced class-action lawsuits (group lawsuits by shareholders) after the stock fell 11.4%.
A company director, William F. Galtney Jr., sold some of his company shares, per insider-trading reports.

takeaways: Everest's investments did well, but its core insurance work lost money this quarter.
Old claims keep costing more than planned. This happened in 2025 and again this year.
Profit fell, disasters hurt, and some shareholders are suing, while share buybacks and dividends continued.

earnings.headline: Profit fell from a year ago, but Edison kept its own full-year 2026 forecast the same.
points: Core profit per share (core EPS) was $1.92, down from $2.34 a year ago. Last year had a one-time catch-up boost.
Net income (profit) was $724 million, down from $832 million in the same quarter last year.
Their own forecast (guidance) for 2026 core EPS stays at $5.90 to $6.20. They still expect 5% to 7% growth from 2025-2030.
Sales got a lift from a rate increase regulators allowed. About 90% of the local grid in high fire risk areas is now hardened.
Main business: Southern California Edison delivers electricity to 15 million people over about 50,000 square miles.
2025 earnings rose $3,175 million, mostly because regulators let them recover past wildfire costs through customer bills.
Core earnings at the utility rose $679 million, helped by higher approved rates and lower interest costs.
Biggest risks they name: wildfires their equipment may start, not recovering costs, credit downgrades and cyberattacks.
One analyst site lowered its rating on the stock, and another wrote about an earnings miss.
Some articles focus on the dividend (cash paid to owners) as a source of passive income.
One report says an investment firm cut how much of the stock it holds.

takeaways: This quarter's profit was lower than last year, partly because last year had a one-time boost.
The company still expects 2026 profit in the same range it forecast before.
Wildfires remain the big risk, and the company is pushing California for lasting wildfire reform.

earnings.headline: Sales grew 7% in the quarter ended September 30, 2026, profit rose sharply, and the company raised its own forecast for the year.
points: Sales rose 7% to $3.7 billion. Fragrance led, up 19%. Hair care was the weak spot, slipping 1%.
Profit per share rose to $.64 from $.13. Operating margin (profit kept per sales dollar) rose to 11.0% from 4.9%.
Free cash flow (cash left after running the business) was still negative $235 million, better than negative $436 million.
They raised their own full-year forecast (guidance) for sales, margin and profit per share, citing cost cuts and new products.
They make money selling skin care, makeup, fragrance and hair care brands like Estée Lauder, Clinique, M·A·C and La Mer.
In fiscal 2025, sales fell 8% to $14,326 million. Asia/Pacific, which includes travel retail (airport shops), dropped 21%.
They had an operating loss of $785 million, with $898 million of write-downs cutting what TOM FORD and Too Faced are worth on paper.
Problems they name: weak shopper mood in China and North America, a $159 million talc lawsuit settlement, and cyberattacks.
Insiders sold shares: director Barry Sternlicht sold 4,697, and Rashida La Lande sold after using 5,564 stock options.
Some articles compare Estée Lauder with rival Coty, and one says the shares already look fully priced after the raised forecast.

takeaways: The business is growing again: sales rose and profit improved a lot compared with a weak quarter a year earlier.
Cost cuts and price increases are a big reason profit rose, not just more sales.
Risks remain: cash flow was still negative this quarter, and last year sales fell and big write-downs hit.

earnings.headline: Elevance Health's sales grew a little and profit per share rose, and it raised its own forecast for the year, but it lost members.
points: Sales (revenue) were $50.4 billion, up 0.7% from a year ago, helped by higher prices, not more members.
Profit per share was $6.27, up 17.9%, but $1.85 per share came from one-off items outside the main business.
Guidance (their own forecast) for 2026 profit per share rose to at least $22.00, or at least $29.00 on an adjusted basis.
Members fell by 487 thousand to about 44.9 million. Medicare Advantage members dropped 15.5%.
One of the biggest US health insurers. It earns money from premiums (insurance fees), employer fees and pharmacy services.
It had about 45.2 million medical members at the end of 2025, under brands like Anthem Blue Cross, Wellpoint and Carelon.
Biggest named risk: medical costs rising faster than the prices they set, which are often fixed for 12 months.
Other named risks: Medicare and Medicaid rule changes, government quality ratings, cyber-attacks and a large amount of debt.
Elevance is suing over a $516M loss tied to Medicare star ratings (government quality scores that affect pay).
Several analysts turned more positive after the raised forecast; one headline says the stock fell 6% as the sector retreated.

takeaways: Profit and the forecast went up, but part of the profit jump came from one-off items, not the core business.
The company is losing members, mostly in Medicare Advantage and Medicaid, and grew mainly by charging more per member.
Its pharmacy and services arm, Carelon, is doing better, with operating gain up 17 percent from a year ago.

earnings.headline: Sales and profit rose versus a year ago, but cash from operations fell and demand is softening.
points: Sales (revenue) rose 8 percent to $2,385 vs $2,202 a year ago (in millions), mostly from charging higher prices.
Profit per share was 2.19 vs 0.60; adjusted (one-time items removed) was 1.84 vs 1.14.
Cash from running the business fell to 290 from 402 (in millions). Fibers profit dropped on lower contract prices.
Their own forecast (guidance): full-year adjusted profit per share of $6.00 to $6.20 and about $850 million operating cash.
Eastman makes specialty materials like plastics, films, additives and fibers that end up in everyday products.
It has 36 factories plus joint ventures in 12 countries; more than half of 2025 sales were outside North America.
It runs the world's largest polyester molecular recycling plant (breaks old plastic down to reuse), started in 2024.
Risks it names: a weak global economy, swings in raw material and energy costs, supply-chain problems, higher interest rates.
Headlines focus on the $375 million U.S. Energy Department award backing its plastic recycling plans.
Several items are stock forecasts or dividend opinion columns, not new company news.
One headline about Euro Manganese shares the EMN symbol but is a different company.

takeaways: Sales grew mainly because prices rose along with costs, not because customers bought much more.
Profit improved this quarter, but cash coming in fell and demand for cars and long-lasting goods is softening.
The company is leaning on plastic recycling for growth, now backed by a reinstated government award.

earnings.headline: Emerson grew sales and profit this quarter, new orders jumped, and it raised its dividend.
points: Sales (money from customers) rose 7% to $5,201 million, up from $4,855 million a year ago.
Profit after tax was $744 million vs $609 million. Taxes rose too, to $253 million from $152 million.
Their own forecast (guidance) for 2027: about 5% sales growth and adjusted profit per share near $7.25.
New orders were up 14%. But Europe barely grew: sales there were up just 1% this quarter.
Several articles debate whether the stock is pricey compared with the cash the business brings in.
One filing shows the finance chief (CFO) now directly holds 147,472 shares after tax withholding.
Other headlines cover daily stock moves, which say little about how the business itself is doing.

takeaways: Emerson sold more and kept more of each sale as profit: its margin rose to 19.2% from 15.6%.
It plans to hand about $3.8B back to owners in 2027 via buybacks and dividends, and raised its dividend 7%.
Not all good: Europe was weak, yearly interest costs rose to $334 million from $237 million, and forecasts can miss.

earnings.headline: Sales held about steady from last quarter, but profit fell and the company expects a weaker next quarter as home solar demand stays soft.
points: Sales (revenue) were $293.3 million, about the same as last quarter but lower than the same quarter a year ago.
Profit (net income) was $23.4 million, down from last quarter and from a year ago. Europe sales fell about 11%.
Their own forecast (guidance) for next quarter: sales of $225.0 million to $255.0 million, lower than this quarter.
U.S. sell-through (sales to end customers) fell 35% from a year ago, in line with a weak U.S. home solar market.
They mainly sell microinverters (small boxes that turn solar panel power into home power), plus batteries and EV chargers.
Big change: a federal home solar tax credit (Section 25D) ended December 31, 2025, which can hurt demand for buying solar.
Risks they name: tariffs, stricter tax-credit rules, and battery cells that come only from two vendors in China.
They warn weak solar demand has caused money trouble, bankruptcies and closures among some installers and distributors.
Several headlines say the stock has fallen along with other solar stocks during a sector selloff.
One headline notes Enphase started building parts in Texas for power systems used in AI data centers.

takeaways: The core home solar business is shrinking for now, and the company itself expects next quarter's sales to drop.
The company still made a profit and holds $931.8 million in cash and investments, which gives it room to adjust.
The AI data center product is promising but early: pilots in 2027, with real sales not expected until 2028.

earnings.headline: EOG made much more money than a year ago, helped by higher oil prices and more oil and gas pumped.
points: Sales were $8,549 million this quarter, up from $5,847 million a year ago, but a bit below $8,620 million last quarter.
Profit (net income) rose to $2,781 million from $1,471 million a year ago. That is $5.33 per share vs $2.70.
Oil sold for $86.72 a barrel vs $65.95 a year ago, and output hit 1,433.1 thousand barrels-equivalent a day.
No new forecast (guidance) in this release. $242 million of profit came from selling assets, a one-off type of gain.
EOG drills for and sells oil, natural gas and gas liquids, mostly in Texas, New Mexico and Ohio, plus Trinidad.
2025 profit fell to $4,980 million from $6,403 million in 2024, while the oil price averaged $64.78, down 14%.
They bought Encino for $5.7 billion in 2025, adding 675,000 acres in the Utica area. Debt rose: 21% of capital vs 14%.
Biggest risk they name: oil and gas prices swing a lot, and tariffs or rising costs could hurt results.
Headlines focus on record oil and gas output and a dividend (cash paid to owners) increase.
Some analysts rate the stock "Hold"; other writers say it may be undervalued. These are opinions, not facts.

takeaways: Higher oil prices this year made EOG much more profitable than a year ago.
Its results rise and fall with oil and gas prices, which the company itself says are hard to predict.
It is spending cash buying back its own shares ($1,063 million this quarter) and paying a $1.0200 per-share dividend.

earnings.headline: EPAM's sales grew a little and profits rose, but cash fell and its own forecast for next quarter is roughly flat.
points: Sales (revenue) were $1.426 billion, up 2.3% from a year ago. That is slow but steady growth.
Profit per share (EPS) was $2.53, up 32.5%. Operating profit rose to 12.3% of sales from 10.4%.
Their own forecast (guidance) for Q4 sales is $1.405 billion to $1.420 billion, anywhere from a slight drop to 0.9% growth.
Worse: cash on hand fell 25.5% to $969.9 million. They plan to borrow to help fund a $500 million share repurchase.
EPAM sells software engineering, AI and consulting work. Most of it is billed by the hour, day or month (time-and-materials).
2025 sales rose 15.4% to $5.457 billion, but 9.2% of that growth came from companies it acquired.
Worse: operating profit slipped to 9.5% of sales from 11.5%, and profit per share fell to $6.72 from $7.84.
Risks they name include the war in Ukraine, shaky world markets and the economy, and how fast clients adopt AI.
Headlines say an activist investor (a big shareholder pushing for changes) is putting pressure on the company.
Several stories focus on the new share repurchase plan and what it could mean for the business.
The stock has moved both ways since results. One story cites a 3.3% pullback, and another a sharp jump.

takeaways: Sales are barely growing now. Their own forecast for Q4 ranges from a slight drop to small growth.
Profits are improving. The company keeps more of each sales dollar than it did a year ago.
Cash is tighter. Nine-month operating cash fell to $250.1 million from $372.0 million, yet they plan big share repurchases.

earnings.headline: Equinix had a strong summer quarter: sales and profit grew, and it raised its own forecast for 2026 again.
points: Sales (revenue) were $2.571 billion, up 11% from the same quarter last year.
Profit was $489 million, up 31%, but part of that came from a one-time fee tied to its atNorth deal, so not all of it will repeat.
They raised their own forecast (guidance) for 2026 sales to between $10.325 and $10.365 billion, the third raise in a row.
New signed deals (bookings) hit a record $533 million a year, up 35%, and they plan nearly 40% more server space this year than first planned.
Equinix rents space, power and connections inside data centers (buildings full of computers), with 280 data centers in 36 countries.
In 2025 it opened 16 new data centers, passed 500,000 connections, and new deals were $1.6 billion, up 27% from 2024.
Building costs money: it raised $4.4 billion in 2025, mostly by borrowing $4.3 billion, and space in use slipped from 78% to 77%.
Big risks they name: rising power costs and shortages, AI chip shortages, tariffs, wars, and customers cutting back in a weak economy.
Several articles say its data center network is hard to copy, and some analysts view the company favorably.
Other stories warn that U.S. data centers face an AI power crunch: there may not be enough electricity to grow.
It opened another data center in Singapore; its sites there have had 100% renewable energy coverage since 2020.

takeaways: Business is growing: more customers, especially for AI, are renting space and connections in Equinix buildings.
Part of this quarter's profit jump was a one-time fee, so the next quarters may not look quite as strong.
The big worry is power: Equinix needs huge amounts of electricity, and costs and shortages could slow it down.

earnings.headline: EQT sold less gas and earned less than a year ago, but kept costs low, cut debt and raised its dividend.
points: Sales volume fell to 583 Bcfe (billion cubic feet of gas equivalent) from 634 a year ago, partly by choosing to hold back 21 Bcfe.
Profit fell: net income for EQT was $279 million vs $336 million a year ago; profit per share fell to $0.44 from $0.53.
Free cash flow (cash left after spending) for EQT dropped to $283 million from $484 million, though spending came in below plan.
Their own forecast (guidance) for next quarter: 550 – 600 Bcfe of sales. They also agreed to buy Range Resources, another gas producer.
EQT drills for natural gas in the Appalachian region and also owns pipelines that move gas, which bring steadier income.
At the end of 2025 they had 28.0 Tcfe of proven reserves: gas, oil and liquids they expect they can pull out of the ground.
Debt dropped to $5.6 billion by September 30, 2026, from $7.8 billion at the end of 2025.
Risks they name: falling gas prices, drilling accidents, bad weather, pipeline damage, permit delays and cyber attacks.
Headlines focus on EQT's all-stock deal to buy Range Resources, meaning EQT pays with its own shares instead of cash.
Some stories say a natural gas price rally and the Range deal have lifted interest in EQT shares.

takeaways: Less gas sold and slightly lower prices meant lower profit and less spare cash than last year. That part got worse.
On the plus side, costs stayed low, debt is down a lot, and the dividend (cash paid to owners) went up 3%.
The big story is the Range deal. It makes EQT much larger, but big mergers carry their own risks.

earnings.headline: Eversource earned less this quarter than a year ago, and its own 2026 forecast is now below what it said in February.
points: Profit was $346.0 million ($0.92 per share), down from $367.5 million ($0.99) in the same quarter of 2025.
Leaving out one-time items, last year's quarter made $1.19 per share, so the core business earned less this time.
Their own 2026 forecast is now $4.62 to $4.70 per share, below the $4.80 to $4.95 they forecast in February.
The gas business lost $43.4 million this quarter, worse than a $16.8 million loss a year ago, mainly from a billing schedule change.
They make money delivering electricity and natural gas to more than 4 million customers in Connecticut, Massachusetts and New Hampshire.
In 2025 they earned $1.69 billion, or $4.56 per share, up from $2.27 per share in 2024, a year hit by big offshore wind losses.
They plan to spend $26.51 billion on wires, pipes and equipment from 2026 through 2030.
Risks they name: cyberattacks on the grid, data leaks, and new AI tools. They say insurance may not cover every loss.
One headline says investors were reacting to an earnings miss, meaning results came in below what analysts expected.
Barclays restarted coverage with an 'Equalweight' rating, which means it sees the company as roughly in line with peers.
A Seeking Alpha piece argues the company's grid spending plan matters more than its risks from regulators.

takeaways: Profit fell this quarter and so far this year, and the company's own 2026 forecast is lower than the one it gave in February.
Regulators set what this company can earn. A lower allowed profit rate and denied storm costs both hurt results this year.
One-time costs from the sale of its water business and old offshore wind deals cut 2026 profit. Management says these are not part of normal operations.

earnings.headline: Core profit per share edged up and they raised their full-year forecast, but net income per share fell versus last year.
points: Sales from the same buildings grew 3.0% vs a year ago; Northern California led at 5.4%, Seattle Metro only 1.3%.
Net income per share fell to $1.52 from $2.56 (last year had property-sale gains); Core FFO per share rose 0.8% to $4.00.
They raised their own 2026 forecast: Core FFO per share now $16.10 - $16.22, and Q3 beat their own forecast by $0.01.
Bad news: building costs rose 6.7% vs last quarter, so profit from the same buildings fell 1.3% vs last quarter.
Essex owns and rents out apartments on the West Coast: 259 communities with 63,077 homes as of December 31, 2025.
In 2025, sales from the same buildings grew 3.3%, mostly because average rent rose to $2,699 from $2,638.
Risks they name: rent control and eviction limits, recessions, falling rents on short leases, costs rising faster than rent.
They also flag AI replacing workers and immigration policy as things that could shrink the number of renters.
Many 'ESS' headlines are about ESS Tech, a different company (a battery maker) that shut down. It is not Essex.
Morgan Stanley, a big bank, lowered its price target (its guess of what the stock is worth) for Essex.

takeaways: Their apartments stayed about 96.3% full, the same as last quarter, so demand for their homes looks steady.
Northern California is the bright spot; Seattle and Los Angeles grew much more slowly.
The company's own forecast went up a little, but costs have been rising faster lately, which squeezes profit.

earnings.headline: Sales grew 15% to $478 million and beat the company's own forecast, but by strict accounting rules it still lost money.
points: Sales (revenue) were $478 million, up 15% from a year ago.
By strict accounting rules (GAAP) they lost $24 million on operations; by their own adjusted measure they earned $77 million.
Their own forecast (guidance) for next quarter: $486 million to $487 million in sales, and a GAAP operating profit.
Signed contracts not yet billed for the next year (cRPO, a backlog) grew 21% to $1.153 billion, faster than sales.
They sell search, security and system-monitoring software, as a cloud service or to run yourself, mostly by subscription.
The $367.8 million profit for fiscal 2026 would have been a loss without a one-time tax accounting gain.
They have lost money in all but two years since they started; total past losses add up to $732.0 million.
Risks they name: tough AI competition, less tech spending if the economy weakens, and costs that keep going up.
Headlines look ahead to next quarter's results and ask if 20% backlog growth is holding up.
One headline points to a 16% slide in the share price.
Elastic is bringing its AI models to Microsoft Foundry, a platform where companies build AI apps.

takeaways: Sales and the backlog of signed future business are both growing steadily.
By standard accounting rules the company still loses money; its profit figure is its own adjusted version.
It bought back about $40 million of its own shares and holds $1.461 billion in cash and investments.

earnings.headline: Entergy earned more than a year ago, helped by hot weather and more power use, and narrowed its own 2026 forecast.
points: Profit (earnings) was $940 million, or $1.98 per share, up from $694 million, or $1.53 per share, a year ago.
People used more power, partly due to hot weather. Weather alone added about $0.24 per share vs $0.06 last year.
Costs rose too: interest on debt, upkeep (O&M) and wear-and-tear (depreciation). The parent company's loss grew to $139 million.
Their own forecast (guidance) for 2026 was narrowed to $4.35 to $4.45 per share. The dividend was raised six percent to 68 cents.
Entergy makes and delivers electricity to more than 3 million customers in Arkansas, Louisiana, Mississippi and Texas.
A big theme: fast-growing power demand from large data centers, which means building more plants and power lines.
Risk: regulators may not let them charge customers for all their costs, or may take longer to approve it.
Risk: if expected data center customers don't show up, money spent to serve them could be hard to get back.
A company officer exercised stock options and sold shares at an average $110.52 each, per a public filing notice.
Entergy presented at an industry finance conference (EEI); some articles ask if the stock price is high compared to its dividend.
The New Orleans unit is spending on grid reliability, the same goal behind the $14 million in federal grants.

takeaways: Profit grew this quarter, but hot weather did a lot of the work, and weather is not the same every year.
Costs like interest on debt are rising while Entergy builds for big new customers like data centers.
The dividend went up six percent, and the company's own 2026 forecast was narrowed, not cut.

earnings.headline: Charging sales grew 29% but total sales slipped 1% and the loss got bigger, while a $2.00-a-share take-private offer is under review.
points: Charging sales (money from drivers plugging in) were $72 million, up 29%. Total sales slipped 1% from a year ago.
Net loss (money lost after all costs) grew 74% vs last year. Gross margin (share of sales kept as profit) rose to 14.9% from 13.6%.
Their own forecast (guidance) for 2026: total sales of $375-$400 million and an adjusted operating loss of $15 million to $30 million.
Surprise: LS Power, already an owner, offered $2.00 a share in cash to take EVgo private. A board committee is reviewing it. Nothing is decided.
They make money mainly by charging drivers for fast EV charging at 1,200+ stations in 47 states, plus deals with carmakers and fleets.
Their network powered more than 1.1 billion electric miles in 2025.
Big risks they name: a history of losses, depending on people adopting EVs, and needing to keep drawing on a government (DOE) loan.
They also warn that government policy changes could hurt them, and that they rely on a small number of equipment vendors and partners.
Headlines say third-quarter sales came in below what Wall Street analysts expected.
Research firms Stifel and Roth/MKM lowered their ratings, pointing to the take-private offer and slower EV growth.
Some coverage focuses on the company's plans to add new charging stalls in 2026.

takeaways: More people use EVgo (over 1.9 million accounts), but the company still loses money, and the loss grew this quarter.
Each public stall was used a bit less on average: 283 kilowatt hours a day vs 295 a year ago.
A $2.00-a-share take-private offer is on the table but not decided, so who will own the company is uncertain.

earnings.headline: Edwards sold more heart devices than expected this quarter and raised its own forecast for the full year.
points: Sales grew 10.5% to $1.72 billion. Aortic valves (TAVR) rose 8.0%; mitral and tricuspid devices (TMTT) jumped 44.0% to $207 million.
Earnings per share (EPS, profit split per share) were $0.53. Adjusted EPS, which strips out one-off items, was $0.80, up 19% from last year.
They raised their own forecast (guidance): 2026 sales growth now about 11.5%, up from 10% to 11%.
Weaker spot: surgical sales grew only 2.5%. They say future growth should come more from more procedures than from winning customers.
They make heart valves and repair devices, used in surgery or put in through a thin tube (catheter) without open-heart surgery.
2025 sales were $6.1 billion, up 11.5%, mostly from TAVR and TMTT products.
But 2025 net income (profit) fell, due to higher staff costs, one-time investment write-downs and higher legal costs.
Risks they name: new products failing, failed clinical trials, factory or quality problems, competition and lower insurance payments.
Headlines say the company beat expectations and raised its outlook, and the stock reached its highest level since 2022.
Some writers warn the stock price may already be high compared with the company's earnings (valuation).

takeaways: The company is growing: more patients are getting its heart valves, and newer devices are growing fastest.
Management now expects a better year than it first predicted, but its own forecasts are not promises.
Not everything improved: surgical sales grew slowly, and 2025 profit fell even though sales rose.

earnings.headline: East West, a bank, set records for sales and profit this quarter, but it also set aside more money in case loans go bad.
points: Sales (revenue) hit a record $823 million, up 4% from last quarter, mostly from interest earned on loans.
Profit was a record $382 million, or $2.76 per share, up 4% from a year ago.
No forecast was given. Citing an uncertain economy, it set aside $45 million for possible loan losses, vs $33 million last quarter.
Bad news: problem assets rose to $256 million from $247 million, and book value per share fell 2% to $65.97.
It mainly earns the gap between interest it charges on loans and interest it pays on deposits (net interest income).
2025 profit was $1.3 billion, up 14% from 2024. Diluted earnings per share rose to $9.52 from $8.33.
Its biggest named risk is interest-rate swings, which can hurt its earnings and the value of what it owns.
It also names tariffs, government shutdowns, a softer job market and a new Fed chair in 2026 as sources of uncertainty.
CEO Dominic Ng sold about $4.57 million of shares, per an SEC filing. Insider sales can happen for many personal reasons.
The bank presented at an industry conference for bank analysts in Boston.

takeaways: The bank is earning more than ever, and customers keep adding money, with no-interest checking deposits up nearly 15% in a year.
Loan losses are still low, but problem assets ticked up and the bank is saving more for possible bad loans.
Fee income dipped 2% from last quarter and the CEO sold shares. Worth weighing next to the record profit.

earnings.headline: Exelon's adjusted profit edged up this quarter, but its official profit fell, and one of its utilities earned much less.
points: Official profit (GAAP) fell to $0.70 per share from $0.86 a year ago. Their own adjusted measure rose to $0.87.
Higher approved rates (the prices regulators let them charge) lifted profit at ComEd, BGE and PHI.
PECO's profit dropped to $165 million from $250 million, mainly from higher storm costs, taxes and interest.
Their own 2026 forecast (guidance) is now $2.85 to $2.91 per share. They declared a $0.42 per share quarterly dividend.
Exelon runs six regulated power and gas utilities serving almost 11 million customers. Regulators set the prices it charges.
In 2025, official profit rose to $2.73 per share from $2.45 in 2024, helped by rate increases, partly offset by higher interest.
They sold about 16 million new shares in 2025 for $691 million. More shares means each existing share owns a bit less.
Risks they name: equipment or storm failures, tax law changes, lawsuits, and bad press making regulators less friendly.
Most headlines are stock price pages and forecasts, not actual company news.
One report says long-term debt was USD 14.32 Billion as of Sept. 30, 2026.
One investor reported holding 59.4 million Exelon shares.

takeaways: This is a slow, steady utility: regulators approve its prices, so profit depends a lot on their decisions.
The core business grew a little, but official profit fell and storm costs hit PECO hard this quarter.
They borrow and sell new shares to pay for grid upgrades; that debt must be repaid and new shares dilute owners.

points: The share price hit a 52-week high, which means its highest price in about a year.
Headlines say the shares rose 10% in 4 days, and the bank's total market value neared ₹11 trn.
Morgan Stanley added ICICI Bank to its focus list. The bank also gave new shares to staff under its employee stock option plan.

takeaways: These headlines are about the share price moving, not about new sales or profit numbers from the bank.
A rising price alone does not show the business got better. No official results were in this source.
When a bank gives new shares to staff, there are more shares in total, so each existing share is a slightly smaller slice.

earnings.headline: Sales hit a record $808.4 million, but profit fell as costs rose and home building stayed weak.
points: Sales (revenue) rose 3.9% to a record $808.4 million, helped by companies they recently bought.
Profit fell: net income was $59.4 million, down from $74.4 million a year ago, or $2.24 a share vs $2.74.
Gross margin (profit kept from each $1 of sales) shrank to 31.8% from 34.0%, hurt by higher fuel and aluminum costs.
At existing branches, home sales fell 2.6% and commercial rose 10.3%. They expect to buy at least $100 million of sales in 2026.
They mainly install insulation in new homes and buildings, from about 250 branches in all 48 continental states.
Insulation was about 58% of 2025 sales of $3.0 billion, down from 60% the year before, as other products grew.
Growth comes from buying others: over 200 companies bought since 1999. Failing to fit new ones in well is a named risk.
Big risks they name: a slower housing market, higher mortgage rates, tariffs, material costs, and their debt.
Headlines say IBP finished a $698 million deal to buy Old Dominion Group, a local contractor.
Analysts disagree: Deutsche Bank upgraded its rating after the deal, while Zacks named IBP its 'Bear of the Day.'
One headline says a smaller insulation deal in Montana adds over $6 million in yearly sales.

takeaways: Sales are growing mostly because the company keeps buying other businesses, not because home building is strong.
Profit is shrinking even as sales grow, because costs like fuel and aluminum went up.
They added $250 million to an existing loan to pay for deals, which means more debt and higher interest costs.

earnings.headline: Sales and profit grew faster than a year ago and they raised their yearly forecast, though quick test-kit sales barely grew.
points: Sales were $1,214 million for the quarter, up 10% from a year ago, led by tests for pet clinics.
Profit per share (EPS) was $4.01, up 18%. But they now expect a slightly lower 2026 profit margin: 32.1% - 32.3%.
They raised their 2026 forecast (guidance): sales $4,741 million - $4,767 million, profit per share $14.96 - $15.16.
Weak spots: quick test-kit sales grew only 1% as fewer tests were run, and sales of lab machines were flat.
They make tests, lab machines and software for vets, plus tests for farm animals, milk and water.
Most money comes from pet clinics: in-clinic test machines and their supplies, outside lab tests, and vet office software.
Risk they name: costs for labor, energy and shipping keep rising, tariffs may add more, and price hikes could lose customers.
A stronger U.S. dollar hurts them since they sell worldwide. They had $398.0 million borrowed on their credit line.
Two insiders sold shares recently: a board member ($844K) and an executive vice president ($2.74M).
On Nov. 16 the executive chair gave away 700 shares as a gift.
Most other headlines are stock-price commentary and analyst forecasts, not news about the business itself.

takeaways: The main pet-testing business is growing, and the company raised its own forecast for the year.
Not everything improved: quick test kits barely grew, machine sales were flat, and the margin forecast went down.
Forecasts are not promises. The company itself points to rising costs, tariffs and a strong dollar as risks.

earnings.headline: Sales rose, but IEP swung to a $225 million loss as refining hedges (bets meant to protect value) lost $522 million.
points: Revenue (sales) was $3.2 billion this quarter, up from $2.7 billion a year earlier.
It lost $225 million, versus a $287 million profit a year ago. Hedge losses of $522 million drove much of it.
Net asset value (their estimate of what it all is worth) rose $865 million to about $3.5 billion, mostly from CVR's stock.
CVR Energy plans to buy two refineries from Marathon Petroleum for $4.2 billion. The $0.50 per unit payout stayed the same.
It's a holding company: it owns businesses in investing, energy, cars, food packaging, real estate, home fashion and pharma.
Carl Icahn and his affiliates own about 86% of the units, so he largely controls what the company does.
He pledged 549,400,539 units for personal loans. A big drop in asset value could trigger margin calls (lenders demanding cash).
In February 2026, CVR Energy sold $1 billion of new bonds (borrowed money) to pay off older debt.
Several headlines say the units fell sharply, including one noting a 6.5% drop.
Seeking Alpha argues the 39% yield makes the stock look cheaper than it really is.
Simply Wall St writes about how keeping the payout steady changed how people view the company.

takeaways: Sales grew, but big losses on protective bets turned the quarter into a loss.
The payout stayed at $0.50, but unless you pick cash by December 11, 2026, you get extra units instead.
One person controls most of the company, and his personal loans are a risk the company itself names.

earnings.headline: IDEX had a record quarter: sales and profit rose, new orders jumped 13%, and the company raised its own forecast for the year.
points: Sales (money from customers) hit a record $952 million, up 8% from a year ago.
Profit per share was $1.95 as reported and $2.33 adjusted (leaving out some one-off items). Both rose 15%.
Guidance (their own forecast) went up: full-year organic sales growth is now 6.5% to 6.8%, up from 5% to 6%.
Not all good: some costs rose faster than prices, and chemical, farm and energy customers bought less.
IDEX owns over 50 businesses that make precise parts: pumps, seals, optics, water systems and rescue tools.
2025 sales were a record $3,457.5 million, up 6%, but only 1% came from growth in businesses it already owned.
Reported profit per share fell 3% to $6.41, partly because interest costs on its debt rose 45%.
Risks they name: bought companies that don't work out, tough competitors, and raw material supply or price swings.
A quarterly dividend (cash paid to shareholders) will be IDEX's 129th in a row.
IDEX presented at an RBC industrial conference; other stories compared it with similar companies.
Some 'IEX' headlines are about a stock exchange or Idex Biometrics: different companies, not this one.

takeaways: This quarter was strong: record sales, higher profit, more orders, and a higher forecast for the year.
Most of the growth comes from one part of the company, tied to data centers, chips, space and defense.
Some areas are still weak: chemical, farm and energy customers bought less, and some costs keep rising.

earnings.headline: Sales and adjusted profit grew this quarter and IFF raised the low end of its 2026 forecast, but it still posted a loss under official accounting rules.
points: Sales were $1.94 billion, up 4% from a year ago, with growth in all three divisions: Taste, Scent and Health & Biosciences.
Under official (GAAP) rules it lost $134 million before taxes, or $0.50 per share. On its own adjusted basis it earned $0.83 per share.
Guidance (their own forecast): 2026 sales of $7.5 billion to $7.6 billion. They expect fourth-quarter profit to be softer, though.
Cash from operations in the first nine months was $820 million, up $288 million. They also finished a $500 million share buyback.
They make flavors, scents, enzymes and food ingredients that other companies put in foods, drinks, soaps, perfumes and supplements.
Sales in 2025 were $10.890 billion, down 5% from $11.484 billion in 2024, partly because they sold off some businesses.
They took a $1.153 billion write-down (admitting a unit was worth less than its value on the books) on Food Ingredients.
Risks they name: tough competition, rising raw material costs, a large debt load, and antitrust investigations and lawsuits.
Bank of America lowered its rating on the stock by two steps, to a negative view.
Several articles discuss the raised sales forecast and what Wall Street analysts think of the company.
IFF opened its first forest lab, where researchers captured scents from 27 plants without picking them.

takeaways: Sales and profit grew in all three divisions this quarter, mostly because customers bought more.
Even so, the company expects a weaker fourth quarter, and it carries a lot of debt.
IFF is reshaping itself by selling Food Ingredients, a deal it expects to close by the end of the second quarter of 2027.

earnings.headline: Illumina's sales and profit grew this quarter, beat its own forecast, and it raised its full-year outlook, helped partly by a tariff refund.
points: Sales (revenue) were $1.13 billion, up 4.2% from the same quarter last year.
Profit (net income) rose to $220 million from $150 million a year ago.
They raised their own full-year sales forecast (guidance) to $4.64-$4.66 billion, from $4.60-$4.64 billion.
A one-time $79 million tariff refund boosted profit. They expect to pass $37 million of refunds back to customers.
Illumina is cutting 51 jobs at its San Diego headquarters.
Board member Keith Meister sold $61M of Illumina stock.
Chinese rival BGI, facing US sanctions, is pointing to Illumina's own business in Xinjiang.

takeaways: Sales and profit grew, and the company did better than it told people to expect.
Part of the profit jump came from a one-time tariff refund, so everyday growth was smaller than the headline.
There are real worries too: job cuts, being blacklisted in China, and a board member selling shares.

earnings.headline: IMAX had its best quarter ever, powered by The Odyssey, which sold over $550 million in tickets worldwide.
points: Sales (revenue) were $175 million, up 64% from a year ago, a company record.
Profit was $117 million, but $36.7 million came from a one-time tax accounting gain, not from ticket sales.
Weaker spot: they installed 32 new theater systems, down from 38 a year earlier.
Next: Dune: Part Three in December and a big 2027 film lineup. They gave no number forecast (guidance) here.
IMAX makes money by converting films to its format and by selling or leasing big-screen systems to theaters, who pay yearly fees.
In 2025 its ticket sales (box office) hit a record $1.28 billion, up 40% from the year before.
It ended 2025 with 1,864 IMAX systems in 91 countries and territories, and owns only one location itself.
Risks they name: strong competition for people's time from home and out-of-home entertainment, plus cyber attacks.
IMAX promoted Giovanni Dolci to a newly created Chief Operating Officer role (the boss of day-to-day operations).
Theater chains Regal and Cinemark refused to show Netflix content on IMAX screens, a sign of friction with theater owners.
IMAX screens drew 34% of Godzilla's global opening, despite being less than 1% of screens.

takeaways: Big hit movies drive IMAX's results. A record film made a record quarter; fewer hits would mean weaker numbers.
Part of the record profit was a one-time tax item, so not all of it will repeat.
Cash looks solid: $641 million available versus $251 million in debt. But new theater installs dipped.

points: Infosys shares fell 2.5% and sat near a 1 month low, even with news about a joint venture (a shared business) in Japan.
Broker CLSA is cautious on Infosys and TCS. It flags worries about slower growth and thinner margins (profit kept from each sale).
Nvidia said its Q3 revenue (sales) jumped 103%, yet Infosys and TCS shares fell. The headline asks why.

takeaways: No earnings report or annual report was in the source, so this covers only recent news headlines.
The headlines are mostly about the share price dropping and outside worries, not about new results from the company itself.
Growth and margin concerns come from an outside broker's opinion, not from Infosys's own forecast.

earnings.headline: Sales fell 7.9% and the company posted a loss, but U.S. results beat its own expectations and its cash pile grew.
points: Sales fell 7.9% to $206.7 million vs a year ago, mainly because U.S. sales dropped over insurance billing-code problems.
They lost $24.4 million, partly from $24.1 million of reorganizing costs. Without one-off costs, profit was $4.1 million.
Guidance (their own forecast): 2026 sales of $850 million to $860 million, a narrower range than the one they gave before.
A new billing code for Inspire V starts January 1, 2028, which should make insurance payments clearer for doctors.
They sell an implant that keeps the airway open during sleep for people with sleep apnea who can't use a CPAP mask.
Most sales are in the U.S. (95.6% in 2025). Hospitals and surgery centers buy it, and insurers pay them back.
2025 was strong: sales of $912.0 million, up from $802.8 million, and profit of $145.4 million.
Biggest risk they name: billing-code confusion could cut doctor pay 10% to 50% and lead doctors to do fewer cases.
A rival, Nyxoah, won a default decision against Inspire in a patent court case.
Several articles discuss the narrowed sales forecast and whether the stock's recent rise can last.
Inspire will present at an investor conference on Dec. 1, with a live stream.

takeaways: Sales and profit are down from last year, mostly due to billing-code trouble, though this quarter improved on the last one.
The company holds $453.1 million in cash and investments and still brings in cash from running the business.
The fix they are counting on, a new billing code, does not start until 2028, so the trouble may linger until then.

earnings.headline: Intel's sales grew 21% to $16.5 billion, but profit by the official count fell, and it expects a smaller next quarter.
points: Sales hit $16.5 billion, up 21% from a year ago. Data center chip sales jumped 78%. PC chip sales fell 5%.
Official profit per share (EPS) fell to $0.60 from $0.90, down 33%. Their adjusted count rose to $0.52 from $0.23.
Their own forecast (guidance) for next quarter is sales of $15.0 billion to $16.0 billion, below this quarter's $16.5 billion.
They raised $23 billion by selling new shares. They also warn the PC slowdown lasts at least through the first half of next year.
Shareholders are suing Intel's CEO and CFO after the stock fell 28.6 percent in one day.
Reports say Intel signed its first outside customer for its most advanced chips. Reports also say the CEO purchased shares after the drop.
Other headlines say the stock has given back about 60% since June.

takeaways: Sales are growing fast, led by chips for data centers, while PC chip sales are shrinking.
Intel itself expects next quarter to be smaller, with official profit per share of just $0.10.
The picture is mixed: a lawsuit and a falling stock on one side, new customers and partners like Oracle on the other.

earnings.headline: IonQ posted record sales of $173.8 million, up 336% from a year ago, and raised its own forecast, but the core business still lost money.
points: Sales (revenue) were $173.8 million, up 336% from a year ago. It was their sixth record quarter in a row.
Official profit was $564.0 million, but it came mostly from a non-cash accounting gain on warrants, not from the business itself.
Leaving out one-off items, the business lost $133.6 million this quarter (adjusted EBITDA). It is still losing money.
Their own forecast (guidance) for 2026 sales rose to $505 million to $515 million. Signed orders not yet delivered: $1.2 billion.
They sell quantum computers and access to them over the cloud (Amazon, Microsoft, Google), plus networking, sensing and security tools.
Yearly losses kept growing: $157.8 million, then $331.6 million, then $510.4 million in the latest full year.
