Total losses since the start reached $1,194.1 million. They expect big losses to continue for the foreseeable future.
Risks they name: no scalable quantum computer yet, sales rely on a few customers, rivals could leapfrog them, recent top-staff turnover.
Headlines show big swings: the stock fell 48% in six months and dropped 8.34% in one day, even after strong results.
One headline reports a sudden leadership shake-up. Another writer says they are losing confidence in the company's story.
Other pieces praise the earnings. These are outside opinions, not official company information.

takeaways: Sales are growing very fast, and the company keeps winning big contracts, including from the U.S. military research agency DARPA.
The business still loses money. The big reported profit was an accounting effect, not cash earned from customers.
It has $3.7 billion in cash and investments, counting $2.0 billion raised by selling new shares in October.

earnings.headline: Sales grew and losses shrank this quarter, but Ionis cut its forecast for its drug TRYNGOLZA by about half.
points: Revenue (sales) was $243 million this quarter, up from $157 million in the same quarter a year ago.
Loss from operations shrank to $130 million from $160 million, but costs rose to $373 million from $317 million.
TRYNGOLZA sales fell to $9 million from $32 million; its 2026 forecast was cut from $100-110 million to about $50 million.
DAWNZERA sales jumped to $37 million, and they kept its $110-120 million yearly guidance (guidance = their own forecast).
They make money selling their own drugs, plus royalties (a cut of sales) and payments from partner drug companies.
In 2025 they earned $944 million in revenue and ended the year with $2.7 billion in cash and short-term investments.
Cash has since dropped to $1.9 billion, mostly from paying back debt and paying for day-to-day operations.
Biggest risk they name: little experience selling drugs on their own. If launches disappoint, the business may be harmed.
Headlines say the stock fell sharply after the TRYNGOLZA forecast was cut, hitting a 52-week low.
One headline reports the stock was down 28.5% after the results, and one firm cut its price target.
Another headline mentions a failed trial for a different drug, pelacarsen.

takeaways: Total sales are growing, helped by DAWNZERA and partner payments, but the company still loses money.
Their big launch, TRYNGOLZA, is selling much slower than they hoped. They say they still believe in it long-term.
Cash is shrinking but still large; they expect to end the year with more than $1.6 billion.

points: Headlines say the stock fell sharply on one day, and analysts lowered their price targets (their guess of what a share is worth).
Some traders bought many put options, which are bets that pay off if the share price falls.
An earnings preview for Q3 2026 is out, so new quarterly results are coming. A film award was won by an actor, not the company.

takeaways: The source here is only headlines. There are no official sales or profit numbers to explain yet.
Recent news is mostly negative: a sharp drop, lower analyst targets, and traders betting on further falls.
The Q3 2026 results, when released, will show how the business is actually doing.

earnings.headline: IQVIA's sales and profit grew in the third quarter, and it raised its own forecast for the full year.
points: Sales (revenue) were $4,428 million, up 8.0% from a year ago. Clinical research sales grew faster than the commercial side.
Official profit (GAAP net income) was $350 million; the adjusted version, which skips some costs, was $557 million.
They raised guidance (their own forecast): 2026 sales now expected between $17,350 million and $17,500 million.
New signed work hit $3.2 billion, up 15%. But a review of stalled trials cut about $2.1 billion from the backlog of future work.
They run clinical trials for drug makers and sell health data and insights; about 30% of sales come in foreign currencies.
In 2025, the data and tech side grew sales 7.6%, while clinical research grew only 4.3% as clients held back.
They spent $1,714 million buying other businesses in 2025 and pay no dividends (cash paid out to shareholders).
Risks they name: most contracts can be ended on short notice, data suppliers could limit data, and privacy laws could tighten.
Headlines note the stock rose 59% in six months, though on some days it lagged its competitors.
An IQVIA executive cashed in $1.24M of company shares, while a fund opened a new $717.3M stake.

takeaways: The business grew in the third quarter, and management raised its own full-year forecast.
The company carries a lot of debt: $13,818 million even after subtracting its cash.
The backlog cut and the gap between official and adjusted profit are worth watching, not just the headline growth.

earnings.headline: Sales jumped as the AI cloud business grew, but the company still lost money and its big $4 billion goal slipped later.
points: Total sales (revenue) rose 66% from last quarter to $228 million, mostly from renting out AI computer power.
It still lost money: a $263 million loss, smaller than the $684 million loss the quarter before.
Bitcoin mining sales fell to $28 million from $67 million as the company shifts away from mining.
Its goal of more than $4 billion a year in AI sales slid from year-end 2026 to January 2027, and may slip to February 2027.
IREN owns its land, power and data centers and rents out AI computing power to big tech firms, AI labs and businesses.
This year it began shutting down Bitcoin mining to move power to AI, aiming to mostly finish by December 31, 2026.
It wrote down $631.7 million in value, mostly old Bitcoin mining machines (a write-down = admitting they're worth less).
Risks it names: raising huge sums of money, building delays that push back sales, and AI chips going out of date fast.
Headlines show big swings: one says the stock fell 67% in 6 months, others report sharp jumps after earnings.
Several stories focus on the delay of the $4 billion revenue goal.
Nvidia's own results dragged down IREN and similar AI cloud firms on one day, per CNBC.

takeaways: The AI cloud business is growing fast: backlog (sales already signed but not yet earned) rose to $20.3 billion.
The company is still losing money, and its biggest goal was pushed back a month or two.
It plans to spend $15 billion more this year; $9 billion is lined up and $6 billion still has to be raised.

earnings.headline: Iron Mountain had a record quarter: sales and profit grew, and it raised its own yearly forecast and its dividend.
points: Sales (revenue) hit a record $2.0 billion, up 13.5% from the same quarter a year ago.
Profit (net income) rose to $129 million, up from $86 million a year ago.
They raised their own forecast (guidance): full-year 2026 sales of $7,950 - $8,020 million. Dividend (cash paid to owners) up 15%.
Worse: debt due within a year jumped to $1,232,903 thousand, up from $216,074 thousand at the end of 2025.
They make money renting storage for records and data, including data centers, plus services like shredding, scanning and IT recycling.
2025 sales grew 12.2%, but profit for shareholders fell 19.7%, hurt by higher interest costs and currency losses.
Interest costs rose to $829.3 million in 2025 because they carried more debt. Currency swings cost $105.6 million.
Risks they name: less paper storage as clients go digital, cyberattacks, data center power costs, and their large debt load.
Headlines focus on the 15% dividend raise and data center revenue growing 34%.
One analyst firm, Jefferies, turned more positive, pointing to data center growth.
Not all coverage is upbeat: one piece says cash flow tells a more cautious story, and another asks why the stock fell.

takeaways: The business is growing fast, led by data centers, and the company now expects an even better year than it first said.
Owners are getting more cash: the quarterly dividend went up 15%.
The big catch is debt: interest costs are rising and much more debt now comes due within a year.

earnings.headline: Sales grew and the company raised its yearly forecast, but its official loss got bigger.
points: Revenue (sales) was $221.6 million, up 14.9% from the same quarter a year ago.
Net loss grew to $29.9 million, from $5.2 million a year ago. Operating costs rose to $197.0 million from $145.6 million.
They raised their own full-year sales forecast (guidance) to $890 million to $895 million, including the VitalConnect purchase.
Part of the profit boost was a one-time tariff refund of about $3.1 million, which is not expected to repeat.
They make money from a 14-day wearable heart patch (Zio) plus software that helps doctors spot irregular heartbeats.
Medicare, the US government health plan, paid about 24% of their total revenue in 2025.
For 2026, Medicare raised its national payment rates for their heart tests, but the company says that may not last.
Named risks: pay cuts from Medicare or insurers, tough competition, and heart monitoring being their only service.
Headlines say the stock fell sharply after the results, with reports of a delay for a Zio MCT product.
Citi lowered its rating on the stock despite the sales growth, according to one headline.
A law firm announced an investigation on behalf of investors. Another headline notes a share buyback program.

takeaways: The core business is growing: more patients are using the Zio heart monitor, and sales rose.
It still loses money on its official books, and that loss got bigger this quarter.
The market reacted badly, a reminder that growing sales alone don't tell the full story.

earnings.headline: Sales jumped 22% and surgeries grew, but official profit fell because of a $450 million one-time lawsuit settlement.
points: Sales (revenue) hit $3.05 billion, up 22% from $2.51 billion a year ago, as more surgeries used their robots.
Official profit fell to $523 million from $704 million, mainly due to a one-time $450 million lawsuit settlement charge.
Leaving out one-time items (non-GAAP), profit rose to $1.05 billion from $867 million.
Their own forecast (guidance): da Vinci surgeries grow about 14% to 15% in 2026, with tariffs costing about 0.9% of revenue.
Hospitals get their surgical robots (da Vinci, Ion), often on lease, then pay again for instruments used in each surgery, plus service.
Newest robot, da Vinci 5, got cleared in Japan and Europe in 2025; 1,231 were installed by December 31, 2025.
Big risk they name: rivals like Johnson & Johnson and Medtronic, plus more competition expected in China.
Weight loss drugs have cut the number of weight-loss surgeries, including ones done with their robots.
Many headlines point out sales grew 22% while the stock is still down this year.
Analysts are debating what the company is fairly worth after mixed Q3 forecast changes.

takeaways: The core business grew: more robots placed (546 vs 427) and more surgeries done.
The profit drop came from a one-time $450 million settlement, which still needs court approval.
Cash fell $1.83 billion to $6.80 billion, mostly spent buying back $2.94 billion of its own shares.

points: Itaú, a big Brazilian bank, released its third-quarter 2026 results under IFRS, a global accounting rulebook.
One headline says profit per share (EPS) came in $0.01 below what analysts expected. A small miss, but a miss.
Another headline calls the Q3 result the most resilient, meaning it held up best, among Brazilian banks.

takeaways: Itaú shared new quarterly results. The headlines give no actual sales or profit totals, so the size of the quarter is unclear.
The news is mixed: one writer says it held up better than other Brazilian banks, but profit per share was a bit below forecasts.
These headlines are opinions and summaries. The company's own full report is the place to check the real numbers.

earnings.headline: ITW grew sales and hit record operating profit in the third quarter, and raised its full-year forecast, though a tornado and some weak units held it back.
points: Sales (revenue) were $4.24 billion, up 4.4 percent. A tornado at two Welding plants cut sales by about $40 million.
Profit from operations hit a record $1.18 billion. Earnings per share (profit per share) rose 7 percent to $3.00.
Guidance (their own forecast): full-year earnings per share of $11.45 to $11.55, raised $0.05 at the midpoint.
Not all good: Automotive OEM, Construction Products and Specialty Products sales shrank vs. a year ago.
ITW makes industrial products and equipment in seven segments, with 88 divisions in 49 countries and about 43,000 workers.
Their '80/20' method: focus on the biggest, best customers and products, and cut the less profitable ones.
Growth plan: invent fixes for key customers' problems ('Customer-back Innovation'); about 21,800 patents granted or pending.
Risks they name include raw material costs, tariffs, interest rates and cyber attacks (none material in 2025, 2024 or 2023).
Many headlines are just stock-price pages and forecasts, not news about the business itself.
Some articles call ITW a quality dividend stock; one says the recovery looks real but the price is high.
MarketWatch noted days when the stock did worse than its competitors.

takeaways: Sales and profit grew and the company raised its forecast, but three of its seven business areas shrank.
It raised its dividend (cash paid to shareholders) 7 percent to $6.88 a year, the 63rd year in a row.
Long-term debt rose to $7,153 million from $6,683 million at the end of 2025; cash dipped to $809 million.

earnings.headline: Jack in the Box sold a bit less and earned a bit less this quarter, though one cleaned-up profit measure rose to $61.2 million.
points: Same-store sales (sales at stores open a year+) fell 1.1%. Fewer customers came in; higher prices made up only part of it.
Revenue (total sales) fell 1.8% to $257.7 million. Profit from the ongoing business slipped to $21.0 million from $22.8 million.
Their own forecast (guidance): about 2,100 restaurants by year end, with about 50 to 60 closures. The dividend has been stopped.
Surprise: taxes took a bigger bite, at a 36.9% rate vs 20.9% a year ago. They also borrowed $500 million to replace older debt.
They earn from their own restaurants plus rent, royalties (a cut of sales) and fees from franchise owners, who run 93% of stores.
Big change: they agreed to sell the Del Taco chain for $115 million in cash, to focus on Jack in the Box.
Sales at existing Jack in the Box stores fell 4.2% in 2025, and they closed 86 restaurants that year.
Risks they name: about 70% of stores are in California and Texas, plus rising wages and food costs like beef.
Most of the headlines are about Jack Henry, a different company, not Jack in the Box.
One headline says JACK stock fell below its two-hundred-day average, a common long-term price trend line.

takeaways: Fewer people are visiting, and higher menu prices only partly made up for it.
The company is shrinking on purpose: closing weak stores, selling Del Taco, and paying down old debt.
Profit dipped and the dividend is gone, so the story now depends on whether the turnaround plan works.

earnings.headline: Sales jumped 20% to $3.68 billion, but profit grew only 2% because costs rose almost as fast.
points: Sales (revenue) were $3.68 billion, up 20%. Without fuel surcharges (extra fees for fuel), sales rose 13%.
Profit per share was $1.82 vs. $1.76 a year ago, up 3%. Rising costs ate most of the sales gain.
Profit fell 22% in dedicated trucking and 76% in home delivery, as driver, insurance and delivery costs rose.
Their own forecast: a full-year 2026 tax rate of about 24.0%. The release gives no forecast for sales or profit.
They move freight by truck and rail across the U.S., Canada and Mexico, and match shippers with outside carriers.
They report five business units: rail containers (intermodal), dedicated trucks, freight brokering, home delivery, truckload.
Biggest risks they name: a weak economy, tariffs, bad weather, fuel costs, and finding enough drivers.
Most of their rail freight runs on BNSF and Norfolk Southern. Trouble at those railroads could hurt results.
Southwest flooding and storms disrupted freight; one headline says the shares fell 3.4% on it.
A new company, Groundtruth, launched with J.B. Hunt to tackle billing problems across the industry.
One analysis says margin pressure (costs rising nearly as fast as sales) may limit the company's upside.

takeaways: The business got busier: sales rose 20%, but higher costs meant profit grew only 2%.
Rail containers and freight brokering did well; dedicated trucking and home delivery made much less profit.
They cut debt to $1.12 billion from $1.60 billion and spent $174 million buying back their own shares.

earnings.headline: J&J's sales grew 5.9% to $25.4 Billion, but profit fell sharply because of a one-time charge for talc lawsuits and two deals.
points: Sales (money from customers) rose 5.9% to $25.4 Billion. U.S. sales grew 9.1%, but international sales grew only 1.5%.
Profit fell 95.9% to $210 million, mostly from a one-time charge to settle talc (baby powder) lawsuits and two deals.
Even leaving out one-time items, adjusted profit per share fell 7.5% to $2.59, down from $2.80 a year ago.
They raised their own forecast (guidance): about $101.2 Billion in 2026 sales and $11.10 adjusted profit per share.
J&J makes money two ways: medicines (Innovative Medicine) and medical devices (MedTech). Medicines were $60.4 billion in 2025.
In 2025 total sales rose 6.0% to $94.2 billion. Cancer drug sales jumped 22.1% to $25.4 billion.
STELARA, a former top drug, lost 41.3% of its sales as cheaper copycat versions (biosimilars) arrived.
They name talc lawsuits as a major risk, and payouts could exceed money set aside. They expect OPSUMIT copycats in 2026.
FDA cleared OTTAVA, a new surgery robot, and approved IMAAVY as the first treatment for a rare blood disorder (wAIHA).
J&J proposed a deal to settle ovarian talc lawsuits and bought Firefly Bio to work on new cancer drugs.
In a study, one CARVYKTI infusion gave 50% of patients five years without treatment for a blood cancer (multiple myeloma).

takeaways: Sales are still growing, led by the U.S. and by cancer medicines.
The huge profit drop was mostly one-time costs, but profit still fell even after leaving those out.
Talc lawsuits and cheaper copycat drugs replacing older hits like STELARA are the big risks to watch.

earnings.headline: Sales and profit dipped versus a year ago that had a big one-time property sale, but hotels set a record and the dividend went up.
points: Sales fell 3% to $156.2 million, mostly because last year had a one-time $41.0 million property sale.
Profit (net income) fell 5% to $36.9 million, but operating income (profit from running the business) rose 16% to $61.5 million.
Hotels and clubs had a record quarter: sales up 9% to $66.0 million, and margins rose to 37% from 35%.
In their Margaritaville home venture, finished sales fell to 67 from 82, but new contracts jumped 49% to 106 from 71.
They make money three ways: selling land and homesites in Northwest Florida, running hotels and clubs, and renting out property.
Hotel and club sales grew 8.1% to $215.4 million in 2025; club members rose to 3,594 from 3,476.
Profit margin at hotels and clubs slipped to 31.1% from 31.5%, due to costs of a new golf course and a reopened clubhouse.
Risk they name: three homebuilders made up about 19.6%, 14.4% and 11.1% of money owed to them, so a few buyers matter a lot.

takeaways: Last year's one-time sale makes this quarter look worse; without it, the core business still grew.
Hotels and clubs keep setting records, while finished home sales in the big joint venture slowed.
They are buying back stock and raised the dividend 13%; shares outstanding are the lowest since 1997.

earnings.headline: Keysight had a record quarter: sales and profit rose sharply, and the company said its full-year outlook improved.
points: Sales (revenue) were $1.85 billion, up from $1.35 billion in the same quarter of 2025.
Profit (GAAP net income) was $397 million, or $2.30 per share, up from $191 million, or $1.10 per share.
Their own forecast (guidance) for next quarter: sales of $1.930 billion to $1.950 billion, about 37% growth.
New orders topped $2 billion for a second record quarter. Costs also rose, and some of their debt now comes due within a year.
They sell design and test tools (hardware, software, services) that engineers use to build new tech, mostly for research.
Sales were $5.4 billion in 2025, up from $5.0 billion in 2024. Profit was $850 million, up 38 percent.
They bought Spirent for $1,415 million and sold off parts of it to meet regulators' conditions.
Risks they name: tariffs, tighter export rules, slowing demand, recession, and conflict outside the U.S.

takeaways: Sales and profit grew a lot versus a year ago, and new orders hit a record.
The company expects growth to continue next quarter, but its own forecasts can turn out wrong.
Keep an eye on the risks they name: tariffs, trade rules, and a possible slowdown in customer spending.

earnings.headline: Kraft Heinz sold less and earned less this quarter, but nudged its full-year forecast up a little.
points: Sales fell 2.0% to $6.1 billion. North America fell 3.4%, but Emerging Markets (fast-growing countries) grew 13.8%.
Operating income (profit from the main business) fell 14.6% to $0.9 billion, hurt by higher costs, bonuses and ad spending.
Guidance (their own forecast): adjusted earnings per share of $2.07 to $2.13 for 2026, up from $2.03 to $2.09 before.
Cash from the business was $3.0 billion so far this year, down 4.1%. They paid $1.4 billion in dividends and bought back no shares.
They sell packaged food and drinks like Heinz, Kraft, Oscar Mayer, Philadelphia and Lunchables. Sales were about $25 billion in 2025.
They had planned to split into two separate companies. Their board has now paused that plan.
They sold their baby and specialty food business in Italy, including the Plasmon brand.
Big risks they name: tough competition, cheaper store brands, and changing tastes, including from weight-loss drugs.
Kraft Heinz expects updated packaging to help its growth in 2027.
Reports say the company is putting a new spin on old favorites like Jell-O and Philadelphia cream cheese.

takeaways: Sales and profits both shrank this quarter, mostly in North America, as costs went up.
The company slightly raised its own forecast, so it now expects the year to be a bit less bad than it said before.
It still makes a lot of cash and keeps paying dividends, but its plan to split in two is on hold.

earnings.headline: KLA's sales and profit grew from last quarter and from a year ago, and beat the middle of the company's own forecast.
points: Sales (revenue) were $4.14 billion, up from $3,658 million last quarter and $3,210 million a year ago.
Profit (net income) was $1.55 billion, or $1.18 per share, up from $1.04 last quarter and $0.85 a year ago.
Their own forecast (guidance) for the December quarter: sales of about $4.7 billion, give or take $200 million.
Not all good: unsold goods and parts (inventory) piled up, and the tax bill rose. Per-share figures reflect a ten-for-one stock split.
KLA makes machines and software that check computer chips for flaws while they are made, so factories waste less.
Service work (maintaining and fixing their machines) was about 23% of total sales in fiscal 2026.
Big risks they name: U.S. rules limiting sales to China, tariffs, and relying on a small group of large customers.
They also warn that chip spending runs in boom-and-bust cycles, and that they carry debt they must repay.
Headlines say KLA's stock rose along with other chip-equipment makers during a broad chip-stock rally.
Writers disagree on price: some say the stock looks expensive compared with its sales, others say it looks about right.
Fewer investors are betting the stock will fall (short interest) than at the August peak.

takeaways: Business is growing: sales and profit were higher than last quarter and a year ago, and the company expects more next quarter.
A lot of the growth is tied to AI chip building, which can slow down if chipmakers cut their spending.
China trade rules, tariffs, and a few big customers are real risks the company itself warns about.

earnings.headline: Sales were roughly flat and core profit dipped slightly, but profit per share rose thanks to lower interest costs and taxes.
points: Sales were $4.1 billion, down 0.4 percent. Organic sales (sales without currency swings or exited businesses) fell 1.3 percent.
Adjusted operating profit (core profit, minus one-off costs) was $677 million, down 0.9 percent. Adjusted profit per share rose 17.2 percent.
Guidance (their own forecast) for 2026 was kept the same. The Kenvue purchase closed the week of this report.
A social media problem in China hurt sales. Organic sales in the overseas personal care unit fell 4.6 percent.
They make everyday care products like Huggies, Kleenex, Scott and Depend, sold in more than 175 countries.
They agreed to buy Kenvue, a consumer health company. Each Kenvue share gets $3.50 cash plus 0.14625 of their shares.
In total they expected to issue about 280 million new shares and pay about $6.7 billion, partly with new debt.
They name these as big risks: rising costs for pulp, oil-based materials and energy, plus cyberattacks and tech failures.
Several articles debate whether the stock is fairly priced, and what has gone wrong lately.
Some writers say savings from combining with Kenvue may lower debt over time but take a while to show up as cash.
One headline covers Arbex, the joint venture that took over their former international tissue business.

takeaways: Sales were about flat this quarter. The core business made slightly less profit than a year ago.
China was a real trouble spot, and costs rose faster than the prices they charge.
Buying Kenvue makes the company much bigger. That brings new opportunity, but also new debt and a lot of merging work.

earnings.headline: CarMax sold many more cars and profit per share jumped, but it made less on each car after cutting prices.
points: Sales (revenue) rose 19.5% to $7.9 billion. They sold 387,735 cars to shoppers and dealers, up 14.7%.
Profit per share was $1.16, up from $0.64 a year ago. That is an 81.3% jump.
Worse: profit on each retail car fell $111 to $2,105, because they cut prices to sell more cars.
Next: they plan to start buying back their own shares again this fiscal year and to share a strategy update on November 3.
They make money selling used cars at set, no-haggle prices, running car auctions, and lending money to car buyers.
Last fiscal year they sold 780,684 used cars to shoppers and 538,203 at auction, from 256 stores.
Their loan business serves about 1.0 million customer accounts, with $16.37 billion in car loans.
Biggest risks they name: tough online competition, hackers stealing customer data, and bad weather closing stores.
Stifel, an investment firm, began covering the company with a neutral "Hold" rating.
Several articles debate whether the company looks cheap next to similar companies.
An investment firm, Kinsale Capital Group, reported owning shares.

takeaways: CarMax is selling a lot more cars again, but it got there by cutting prices, so it keeps less on each car.
Its car-loan arm earned more, but it set aside more money for loans that may not get paid back.
The company aims to cut $200 million in yearly costs by the end of fiscal 2027.

earnings.headline: Expand Energy made a $519 million profit this quarter and kept buying back shares, but the release gave no sales comparison.
points: Profit was $519 million, or $2.24 per share. Adjusted profit, which leaves out one-time items, was $338 million.
Cash brought in from running the business was $1,177 million. The release did not give a total sales number for the quarter.
Guidance (their own forecast): about $3 billion of spending in 2026, and $80 million of marketing profit next quarter.
Debt was $4.6 billion. They spent $305 million buying back their own shares and bought Twin Eagle, a gas-trading business.
They make money drilling for and selling natural gas, plus some oil and NGLs (liquid fuels that come out with gas). It is mostly gas.
Sales from gas, oil and NGLs rose $5,507 million in 2025, mostly from buying Southwestern Energy and from higher gas prices.
Costs rose too: moving and processing gas cost $1,341 million more in 2025. The board replaced the CEO in February 2026.
Biggest risks they name: big swings in gas prices, lower demand, drilling accidents, limits from their debt, wars, and new climate rules.
One headline says the stock hit a 52-week low (its lowest price in a year) at 83.24 USD.
Barclays, a big bank, cut its price target for the stock. Other headlines cover the new CEO and analyst forecasts.
One headline says the company expects U.S. natural gas demand to rise over 10% by 2028.

takeaways: The company made a profit and brings in a lot of cash, but its cash on hand dropped sharply since the end of 2025.
It plans to pay a $0.575 per share dividend (a cash payment to owners) on December 3, 2026, and it keeps buying back shares.
Its results depend on gas prices, which swing a lot. The stock was near a one-year low, and a new CEO is now in charge.

earnings.headline: Sales hit a record, but higher fuel and operating costs pushed operating profit down in both main businesses.
points: Sales (revenue) hit a record $652.7 million. Profit after all costs (net earnings) was $111.5 million, or $3.63 per share.
Cement and concrete operating profit fell 12% to $113.0 million. Concrete and gravel profit alone dropped 47% on higher costs.
They sold 7% more wallboard (drywall), but its net price fell 10%. Pricier diesel for trucking hurt every business line.
Office and admin costs rose 26%. Their outlook: high interest rates and economic uncertainty may keep hurting construction near term.
They make cement and gypsum wallboard (drywall) for roads, homes and buildings, from more than 70 sites in 21 states.
Last fiscal year they bought back 1,739,625 of their own shares, paying an average of $219.48 each.
Big risks they name: less government road spending, higher interest rates, bad weather, and commodity price swings.
They warn the U.S. wallboard industry still has a lot of extra factory capacity, which can push prices down.
Headlines focus on the quarter's record sales alongside softer profit per share.
Other coverage recaps what management said on its earnings call about costs and demand.

takeaways: Business was busy: they sold a record amount of cement, but it cost more to make and ship, so profits shrank.
Home building is weak because of high interest rates; road work and big building projects are holding demand up.
They keep buying back stock, about $146.0 million in the first half of the year, and carry $1.5 billion in net debt (debt minus cash).

earnings.headline: Fastenal's sales grew 15.5% in the third quarter of 2026 and profit grew even faster, though it kept a smaller slice of each sale.
points: Sales (money from customers) rose 15.5% to $2,463.3 million, mostly from bigger customers, price increases and steady demand.
Net income (profit after all costs) rose 19.7% to $401.6 million. They returned $328 million to owners via dividends and buybacks.
Worse: gross margin (share of each sale left after product costs) slipped to 44.8% from 45.3%, since big customers pay lower prices.
Worse: they lowered their 2026 goal for new vending/bin machine signings to 27,000 to 29,000, down from 28,000 to 30,000.
Fastenal sells fasteners, safety gear and tools to factories and builders, often through vending machines and bins at customer sites.
In 2025 sales rose 8.7% to $8,200.5 million and profit rose 9.4%, mostly by winning business from rivals, not a stronger economy.
Small customer sites (under $5k a month) fell 11.2%, while big $50k+ sites grew 14.0% as they focus on larger buyers.
Risks they name: tariffs, interest rates, inflation, currency swings and a possible recession; they say the impact cannot be predicted.
Several articles note the stock is up 35% in 2026 and ask whether its dividend (cash paid to owners) still makes sense.
Yahoo Finance reports Fastenal raised its dividend twice in 2026, but says some Wall Street analysts remain unconvinced.

takeaways: Sales and profit grew faster this quarter than last year, mainly by winning more work from big customers.
The trade-off: big customers get better prices, so Fastenal keeps a slightly smaller share of each sale.
Tariffs and a weak economy are named risks, and they trimmed one of their own growth goals for this year.

earnings.headline: Fate still has no product sales and spent more cash, but early lupus data looked good and it won a $15.0 million grant.
points: No product sales yet: it is still testing its drugs. Spending (operating expenses) was $32.2 million this quarter.
Cash and investments fell by $14.7 million to $139.1 million. They expect that cash to last to mid-2028.
Early lupus kidney data: 100% kidney response in the chosen regimen, but only a tiny group (n=2) had Month 6 results.
Side effects across 29 patients: no deaths. Serious infections in 2 patients (6.9%), low blood counts in 6 patients (20.7%).
They make cell treatments from lab-grown stem cells, meant to be ready-made ('off-the-shelf'), not built from each patient's own cells.
They have never made a profit and expect losses to continue. Money comes from selling stock, loans, partners and grants.
Big risk they name: their drugs may fail testing or not get FDA approval, and early data may change as more results come in.
They will need more money. Raising it by selling new shares could shrink current owners' slice (called dilution).
A Form 424B5 filing dated 13 November appeared. This type of filing is used when a company offers new shares or other securities.
One headline says FATE stock was down 14% on one day. The headline does not explain why.

takeaways: This is an early-stage drug company with no product sales. Its future depends on its trials working and getting FDA approval.
Early lupus results and side-effect data look encouraging, but they come from small groups of patients and could change.
Cash keeps shrinking each quarter. They cut spending by $18.5 million over nine months, but may still need to raise more money.

earnings.headline: Sales slipped and the company lowered its own forecast for the year, while it sells or shuts weak parts of the business.
points: Sales were $1.1 billion this quarter, down 3.1 percent from a year ago.
Official profit per share (EPS) was $0.42, pulled down by a $0.47 write-down on assets that lost value.
Adjusted EPS was $1.14, but that got help from a $0.28 one-time tax benefit and $0.14 of tariff refunds.
They cut their full-year forecast: adjusted EPS now $3.20 to $3.30. The middle was $3.37 and is now $3.25.
They sell home products: faucets (Moen), entry doors (Therma-Tru), locks and safes (Master Lock), and decking.
Sales fell 3.2% in 2025. New home building dropped about 6%, and they say most of their market is repairs and remodels.
Biggest risks they name: a slow housing market, interest rates, tariffs (import taxes), and rising costs.
They owed about $2.2 billion in bonds (long-term loans) and extended a backup credit line to January 2031.
Several stories say the stock jumped after the results, while others question whether it is already fully priced.
Coverage focuses on the leadership overhaul: a new finance chief, tech chief and legal chief, plus new business heads.
One opinion piece argues 2027 could be the low point for earnings. That is a writer's view, not a company forecast.

takeaways: The CEO says results are "not where they need to be" and calls this the early stage of a multi-year turnaround.
They are selling the Fiberon decking unit and leaving China; those units lose about $50 million to $55 million a year.
Cash is a bright spot: $331.1 million of free cash flow this quarter, but they expect the next quarter's sales to be lower.

earnings.headline: Profit rose because copper sold for much higher prices, but they sold less copper and gold and costs per pound went up.
points: Sales (revenue) were $7,546 million, up from $6,972 million a year ago, mostly because copper sold for $6.54 a pound vs $4.68.
Profit was $1.2 billion, or $0.81 per share, up from $0.46 per share a year ago.
But they sold less metal: 749 million pounds of copper vs 977, and 105 thousand ounces of gold vs 336, as Grasberg restarts.
Cost to make a pound of copper rose to $2.07 from $1.40. Their own forecast: $1.90 for 2026 and more gold sold in the fourth quarter.
They make money digging up and selling copper, gold and molybdenum (another metal) from mines in Indonesia and the Americas.
A mud rush (a flood of wet mud) hit their big Grasberg mine in Indonesia in September 2025. Restarting it slowly is the big story.
Risks they name: metal prices falling, their debt, and labor, safety and political problems at their mines.
Their Indonesia mining license runs to 2041. They warn that failing to win an extension is a risk.
The stock fell nearly 7% in one day as copper prices kept dropping.
One firm, Erste Group, lowered its rating on the stock (a downgrade).

takeaways: This quarter's bigger profit came mostly from high metal prices, not from selling more metal.
Their biggest mine is still recovering from a 2025 accident, so they made and sold less copper and gold than a year ago.
Because profits ride on copper prices, a drop in copper can hit the company fast, as the recent slide in the stock shows.

earnings.headline: Sales grew 6.3% to $634.7 million in Q4, but reported profit fell as one-time and pay costs rose.
points: Sales rose 6.3% to $634.7 million. Organic ASV (yearly subscription value, without deals) hit $2,568.2 million, up 7.0%.
Profit per share fell to $3.41 from $4.03. Leaving out one-time items, it rose to $4.52 from $4.05.
Operating margin (share of sales kept as profit) dropped to 24.7% from 29.7%, mostly from restructuring and bonus pay.
Their own forecast for fiscal 2027: sales of $2,600 to $2,625 million, subscription growth of 5.0% to 6.5%, slower than 7.0%.
FactSet earns money from subscriptions to financial data, analytics and AI tools, used by 9,200+ clients and 260,000+ users.
Yearly sales were $2,476.3 million, up 6.7%. Net income (profit) fell 10.6% to $533.5 million.
Costs rose from restructuring, higher bonus pay and one-time CEO pay. Spending on new products reached $346.1 million.
The risk section was not in the text provided. Higher pay costs are what squeezed profit margins this year.
Headlines note a 27% stock gain and debate whether the price is now fair.
One headline says worries that AI could disrupt FactSet's business have eased somewhat.
Another says FactSet repeated its 2027 outlook (its own forecast).

takeaways: Sales and subscriptions keep growing. Yearly sales have risen 47 years in a row.
Reported profit fell this year, mostly from one-time and pay costs. Profit without those items still rose.
They expect slower subscription growth next year: 5.0% to 6.5%, compared with 7.0% this year.

earnings.headline: Sales and underlying profit grew, but reported profit fell because of a big one-time loss on its FedEx Freight stake.
points: Sales (revenue) were $22.9 billion this quarter, up from $20.4 billion a year earlier.
Reported profit fell to $0.29 billion from $0.65 billion, mostly due to a $1.2 billion loss on its FedEx Freight stake.
Leaving out one-time items, profit per share rose to $3.74 from $2.93.
Their own forecast (guidance) for 2026 sales growth rose to ~12% from ~11%. Shipping rates rise an average 5.9% on January 4, 2027.
FedEx makes money moving packages and freight worldwide, with annual revenue (sales) of $90 billion and more than 450,000 workers.
This year it split off FedEx Freight into a separate company and kept a 19.9% stake in it.
It pays a $1.22 per share quarterly dividend (cash to owners). Stock buybacks fell to $776 million from $3.0 billion.
Risks it names include tariff and trade changes, fuel prices, labor costs, tough competition, and data breaches.
Several headlines debate whether the stock is fairly priced now that profit margins are improving.
Interim finance chief Claude Russ sold $5.3 million of FedEx stock.
Morningstar says fuel surcharges are lifting sales at FedEx Freight, the business FedEx spun off.

takeaways: The core business is growing: more packages, higher prices, and cost cuts lifted results.
Reported profit dropped this quarter, mainly from a one-time loss on the Freight stake, not from daily operations.
Rising wages, outside transport costs, and trade rules still ate into part of the gains.

earnings.headline: Sales and profit rose from a year ago, and FirstEnergy kept its own forecast for the full year.
points: Revenue (sales) was $4.6 billion this quarter, up from $4.1 billion a year ago.
Profit per share was $0.96, up from $0.76. Core earnings (profit minus one-off items) were $0.98 vs $0.83.
Guidance (their own forecast) for 2026 core earnings stays at $2.62 to $2.82 per share, at or slightly above the middle.
Deals with big power users reached 7.9 gigawatts, nearly double since the start of the year. Legal and investigation costs continued.
They deliver electricity over local wires to over six million customers in the Midwest and Mid-Atlantic.
They also run more than 24,000 miles of transmission lines (big high-voltage lines) and some power plants in West Virginia.
Big risk: a lobbying scandal. In 2021 they paid a $230 million penalty and must still follow a deal with prosecutors.
They expect to lose money on a shareholder lawsuit but can't yet say how much. Weather, rules and borrowing costs are risks too.
Most headlines are stock-price forecasts and analyst opinions, not new company news.
Some valuation sites argue the stock could be 7% to 9% undervalued after the plan to raise grid spending by 25%.
The company presented at an industry finance conference this month.

takeaways: Sales and profit both rose versus last year, and the company kept its yearly forecast.
Its growth plan rests on spending $36 billion over five years to upgrade the power grid.
An old lobbying scandal still brings legal costs and an open shareholder lawsuit. That risk hasn't gone away.

earnings.headline: Sales jumped 27% to $657.0 million, mostly from charging more for mortgage scores, but FICO gave no forecast for next year.
points: Revenue (sales) was $657.0 million, up from $515.8 million a year ago, an increase of 27%.
Profit was $175.0 million, or $8.12 per share, vs $6.42. It includes a $65 million lawsuit settlement and $27 million for job cuts.
Score sales to businesses rose 39%, mainly from a higher price per mortgage score, while the number of new mortgages fell.
No guidance (their own forecast) for fiscal year 2027: mortgage pricing is changing and high interest rates are hurting home loans.
Lenders pay credit bureaus for each FICO Score (a 300-850 credit number); the bureaus pay FICO a fee. It also sells decision software.
Long-term debt nearly doubled this year, and it spent heavily repurchasing its own stock. On paper it now owes more than it owns.
Biggest named risk: rival scores like VantageScore, owned by the three credit bureaus, are gaining approval in U.S. mortgages.
Other risks: customers building their own scores with AI, product bugs or delays, and customers pushing back on its pricing.
Headlines report an earnings miss, a downgrade from RBC, and analysts cutting targets over mortgage uncertainty.
One article says the 72% mortgage jump came from higher prices, not more loans; another says shares are down 55%.
One headline says CEO Will Lansing sold $183,750 in stock.

takeaways: Sales and profit grew a lot, but much of it came from raising prices on mortgage scores, not from more home loans.
The company won't give a forecast for next year, so even it is unsure what comes next.
It carries much more debt and faces a lawsuit settlement, job cuts, and growing competition from VantageScore.

earnings.headline: Five Below's sales jumped 22.9% to $1.26 billion last quarter, and it raised its full-year forecast.
points: Sales rose 22.9% to $1.26 billion. Sales at stores open a year or more (comparable sales) grew 14.1%.
Profit was $221.4 million, much of it one-time tariff refunds. 'Adjusted' profit, without those, was $93.4 million vs $44.8 million.
Guidance (their own forecast) for the year rose to $5.63 billion to $5.71 billion in sales, up from $5.40 billion to $5.48 billion.
Next quarter they expect slower growth: comparable sales of +8% to +10%, down from 14.1% this quarter.
They run value stores selling fun items for kids and adults, most priced at $5 and below, plus online sales.
Comparable sales rose 12.8% in fiscal 2025 after falling 2.7% in fiscal 2024. They had 1,921 stores at year end.
They aim for more than 3,500 stores over time, but say new stores may do worse or pull shoppers from older stores.
Risks they name: inflation, tariffs on goods made overseas, and failing to pick products shoppers want.
Headlines focus on the stock's big run, with one saying it looks stretched after a 69% one-year gain.
Several articles compare Five Below with other retailers like GameStop and Etsy as growth stocks.

takeaways: The business is strong right now: more stores, more shoppers, and a higher forecast for the year.
The giant profit number is boosted by one-time tariff refunds; the adjusted numbers show the everyday business.
They expect growth to slow next quarter, and tariffs and inflation remain real risks.

earnings.headline: Sales grew 25.1% and profit jumped, but a large part of that profit came from a one-time tax benefit.
points: Sales (revenue) rose 25.1% to $250.3 million, up from $200.1 million a year earlier.
Profit was $74.5 million vs $29.6 million, but about $39.2 million was a one-time tax benefit they say won't repeat.
Gross margin (the share of sales kept after direct costs) slipped to 61.0% from 62.3%. That part got worse.
They raised their own forecast (guidance): core sales growth of 25-27% for the year, but Q4 slows to 14-20%.
Flywire makes money helping schools, hospitals, travel firms and businesses get paid by customers around the world.
It pairs a payments network with software made for each industry, like invoicing and flexible payment plans.
B2B (business-to-business payments) is still a fairly new area for them, and they bought a company called Sertifi.
Risks they name: U.S. immigration and visa rules that could cut foreign students, currency swings, competition, and wars.
Headlines focus on the raised yearly forecast and the stock hitting a 52-week high after a 59% run.
Insiders sold some shares, including Mohit Kansal selling 6,053 shares, per MarketBeat.
The CFO (finance chief) will do a live webcast talk in December.

takeaways: The business is growing fast: sales and the money it moves for customers both rose by about a quarter from last year.
The big profit number is boosted by a one-time tax item. Profit from day-to-day business also grew, but less dramatically.
Their own forecast expects slower growth next quarter, and student visa rules are a real risk they point to.

earnings.headline: Sales fell 23% but profit rose 25%, and the company lowered its own 2026 sales forecast.
points: Sales dropped 23% from a year ago to $1.23 billion, mainly because they sold fewer solar panels to other companies.
Profit went up: $571 million, or $5.30 per share, compared with $456 million a year earlier.
They cut their 2026 forecast (guidance) for sales to $4.6B to $4.9B, down from $4.9B to $5.2B before.
Cash minus debt fell to $1.5 billion from $2.4 billion. The board OK'd buying back up to $500 million of the company's own stock.
They make and sell solar panels without using Chinese silicon supply chains, with factories in the U.S., India, Malaysia and Vietnam.
In 2025, sales rose 24% to $5.2 billion, mostly because they sold more panels.
They kept less of each sale: gross profit fell to 40.6% of sales from 44.2%, due to tariffs, shipping and storage costs.
Biggest risks they name: cheap competing panels, changes to government tax credits and tariffs, and losing big customers.
Several headlines say the stock has been falling, one says it was down 15% over 5 straight days.
Some headlines link the stock's moves to politics and hopes for clean energy policy.

takeaways: The company sold fewer panels this quarter but still earned more profit than a year ago.
Their own forecast for 2026 sales went down, so they now expect a smaller year than they first planned.
Much of their business depends on U.S. government rules like tax credits and tariffs, and those rules can change.

earnings.headline: Fortinet's sales grew 20% from a year ago, and the company raised its own forecast for 2026.
points: Sales (revenue) grew 20% from a year ago to $2.08 billion. Sales of physical products jumped 37% to $765 million.
Profit: 34% of sales was left as operating profit under the official rules (GAAP). Earnings per share were $0.86.
Their own forecast (guidance) for next quarter is sales of $2.155 billion to $2.245 billion.
Watch: unsold gear on hand (inventory) rose from 399.5 to 591.2, in millions of dollars, since December 31, 2025.
They sell cybersecurity: firewall gear, software and cloud services that protect networks, devices and data.
Customers are in over 100 countries. They held 1,405 patents worldwide, 321 of them AI-related, as of December 31, 2025.
Big risks they name: results can swing a lot, tariffs, chip shortages, wars, and flaws or hacks in their own products.
They warn that if these risks happen, investors may lose some or all of their investment.
Headlines cover the earnings beat and a stock jump of 5.87% on Nov 18.
Some headlines mention a selloff, and others compare Fortinet with rival CrowdStrike (CRWD).
Writers ask whether its security-operations (SecOps) business will matter more for the company's future.

takeaways: The company grew sales and made solid profit last quarter, and it raised its own forecast.
It is buying back its own shares. It added $1.2 billion to that plan, leaving $2 billion approved.
Forecasts are not promises. Unsold inventory went up, and the company lists many real risks.

earnings.headline: GATX earned more this quarter than a year ago and now expects the full year to come in a bit above its own forecast.
points: Profit rose to $105.2 million, or $2.92 per share, up from $82.2 million, or $2.25 per share, a year earlier.
They now expect 2026 earnings per share a bit above the top of their own forecast (guidance) of $9.90 to $10.30.
Engine Leasing profit fell to $51.4 million from $60.4 million, though last year had a one-time boost of $10.9 million.
Price increases on renewed railcar leases slowed to 12.4%, down from 22.8% a year ago. Fleet use was 98.4% vs 98.9%.
GATX makes money by renting out (leasing) railcars, aircraft spare engines and tank containers to customers worldwide.
Profit depends on renting assets at good rates and renting them again when each lease ends.
Biggest risk they name: customers needing fewer railcars or engines due to inflation, high interest rates or a weak economy.
Railroad changes could hurt: faster trains free up spare railcars, and worse service can push shippers to trucks.
GATX sold $300 Million of senior notes, which is long-term borrowed money (bonds) the company must pay back with interest.
Two insiders sold shares: director Anne L. Arvia sold $173,585 worth and controller Jennifer McManus sold $563,867.

takeaways: The rail leasing business is strong right now: profit rose and nearly all of its railcars are rented out.
Some things are cooling: lease price increases are smaller than last year and engine leasing profit dipped.
The company raised its own outlook, but forecasts can miss; it names risks like a weak economy and high interest rates.

earnings.headline: Sales rose 12.9% to $14.6 billion and profit per share rose 15.7%, but cash left over fell and one unit earned less.
points: Sales (revenue) were $14.6 billion, up 12.9% from a year ago. All four business units sold more.
Profit per share (EPS) was $4.49, up 15.7%. Net earnings were $1,229 million.
New orders hit $98.8 billion, mostly Navy submarines. Backlog (work ordered but not yet done) is $220 billion.
Weaker spots: Combat Systems profit fell 1.5%, and free cash flow (cash left after investing) fell to $1,229 million from $1,897 million.
They make business jets (Gulfstream), Navy ships and submarines, combat vehicles and weapons, and tech services.
About 70% of sales come from the U.S. government, so results depend heavily on defense budgets.
New this year: the G800, their longest-range jet, entered service in 2025, and a new G300 jet was announced.
Risks they name: budget delays or shutdowns, the government canceling contracts, and audits that can bring penalties.
Headlines focus on new Navy work and whether the stock is fairly priced versus rivals like Lockheed Martin and GE.
One report says a company officer sold about $4.84 million of stock.
Their tech unit, General Dynamics Information Technology, got a $23M government contract payment.

takeaways: Sales, profit and orders all grew this quarter, led by Navy submarine work.
Not everything improved: cash left after investing fell, and Combat Systems earned less than a year ago.
Most sales come from the U.S. government, so budget fights in Congress are the big risk to watch.

earnings.headline: GE Aerospace's sales and orders grew fast and it raised its 2026 forecast, but cash coming in from the business fell 14%.
points: Sales (revenue) were $14.1B, up 16%. New orders for engines and service jumped 49% to $19.0B.
Profit was $2.8B, up 12%. But the share of each sales dollar kept as profit slipped to 19.9%, down from last year.
Cash from day-to-day business was $2.2B, down 14% from a year ago. Free cash flow (cash left after spending) fell too.
They raised their own 2026 forecast (guidance): adjusted profit per share of $8.00 - $8.10, up from $7.65 - $7.85.
A report says the CEO plans to sell $95M of his own shares, and a bank, BNP Paribas, warned growth may be slowing.
Several headlines are about GE Vernova, a separate company. They are not about GE Aerospace.
Other headlines debate the stock price and whether to buy. This summary does not take a side on that.

takeaways: GE Aerospace makes and repairs jet engines. Demand is strong: orders, sales and profit all grew this quarter.
Not everything got better: cash coming in fell, the profit margin slipped, and an old insurance unit lost money.
Much of its business is repairs and parts. It says it has over $170 billion of service work already lined up.

earnings.headline: GE HealthCare's sales and profit grew faster than it expected this quarter, and it raised its own forecast for the full year 2026.
points: Sales (revenue) were $5.5 billion, up 7.2% from a year ago, with growth in every part of the business.
Profit (net income) rose to $615 million from $446 million. Profit per share was $1.36, up from $0.98.
They raised their own full-year forecast (guidance): adjusted profit per share now $4.95 - $5.05, up from $4.80 - $5.00.
Cash fell to $2.9 billion and debt is $10.0 billion. They also plan to purchase SOFIE Biosciences for $945 million in cash.
They sell medical scanners, drugs used during scans, repair service and AI software to hospitals in over 160 countries.
Tariffs (import taxes) cut their operating profit by about $245 million in 2025, and they expect that impact to continue.
In China, local rivals and government bulk-purchase rules have hurt their orders and sales, and may keep doing so.
Other risks they name: tough competition, hospital cost cuts, supply problems, cyberattacks, and their debt.
Several articles debate whether the stock is fairly priced after the raised forecast. Opinions differ.
MarketWatch reported the stock fell on some days and did worse than the overall market.
Other stories cover new products and research, like a brain imaging alliance and photon-counting CT scanners.

takeaways: The business grew this quarter, and the company now expects a better year than it said before.
Cash dropped and debt is large, partly from acquiring other companies. That is a cost worth watching.
Tariffs and tougher competition in China are real risks the company itself warns about.

earnings.headline: Extra Space rented slightly more space, cut store costs, and grew profit per share, though some costs like property taxes kept rising.
points: Sales at stores open both years rose 2.7% and costs fell 1.8%, so profit from those stores grew 4.6%.
Core FFO (a key REIT profit measure) was $2.17 per share, up 4.3%. Plain profit rose 50.0%, helped by a weak last year.
Weak spots: property taxes rose 4.9%, other income dipped, and selling some stores led to a $5.8 million loss.
They spent $327.1 million buying back their own shares. Noah Springer becomes CEO on January 1, 2027.
They rent storage units month to month and run 4,281 stores in 43 states plus Washington, D.C.
They also earn fees managing 1,856 stores for other owners, lend money to store owners, and insure tenants' stored goods.
As a REIT (a property company), they must pay out at least 90% of taxable income to shareholders.
Risks they name: more new storage sites competing, rising property taxes, a weak economy, and natural disasters.
Analysts disagree: Truist raised its price target and Morningstar sees demand rebounding, but Benzinga lists it as a risk.
Headlines say profit growth at existing stores is slowly picking up and the company raised its own forecast (guidance).
Several articles compare its dividend and value with rival Public Storage.

takeaways: The business is steady: more space rented and lower store costs, but sales growth is modest at 2.7%.
Not everything improved: property taxes keep climbing and some store sales lost money.
A new CEO takes over January 1, 2027, and the company is spending heavily to buy back its own shares.

earnings.headline: Sales grew 9.5% and Ferguson raised its full-year forecast, but reported earnings per share fell 4.9%.
points: Sales (money from customers) hit $9.0 billion, up 9.5%. About 7.0% came from existing business, the rest mostly from buying companies.
Operating profit was $885 million, up 4.9%. But earnings per share fell 4.9% to $3.08, mostly due to a tax benefit last year.
Guidance (their own forecast) went up: they now expect about 7% sales growth this year, helped by buying FloWorks.
Weaker spots: gross margin (share of each sale kept) dipped to 30.9%, Canada sales fell 4.5%, and debt rose to 1.7x from 1.0x.
Ferguson is a middleman: it buys plumbing, heating, cooling and water products and sells them to contractors. The US is 95% of sales.
Last year sales rose 3.8% to $30.8 billion, but operating profit fell 1.7%, hit by $80 million of one-time cleanup costs.
Earnings per share rose 9.3% to $9.32, mostly because the year before carried a big one-time tax charge.
Risks they name: weak home building, high interest and mortgage rates, tariffs, and a shortage of skilled tradespeople.
Headlines say Ferguson beat expectations and raised its forecast; some writers ask whether the stock already reflects that.
A filing shows an officer, James A. Paisley, proposed selling 2,300 shares.
Several pieces cover what Wall Street analysts think, which is opinion, not company news.

takeaways: The business grew even though home building is weak, mostly from commercial and big projects (non-residential sales up 15%).
Part of the growth is bought: eleven deals this year, worth about $1.5 billion in yearly sales, paid for partly with new debt.
Not everything improved: per-share earnings, margins and Canada slipped, and buybacks are paused while they lower debt.

earnings.headline: FMC's sales collapsed and it lost $2.07 billion as it cut prices and rebates to clear out products stuck with sellers.
points: Sales were $106 million, down $436 million from a year ago, after about $639 million in price and rebate fixes.
Net loss (money lost) was $2.07 billion, mostly from non-cash write-downs plus the price and rebate changes.
Even without India and the fixes, sales fell 22 percent as stores that resell to farmers sharply cut orders late in the quarter.
One bright spot: cash from operations was $7 million, up $191 million from a year ago. Their fourth-quarter forecast was lowered.
FMC sells farm chemicals that kill bugs, weeds and fungus, plus biologicals and plant nutrition products.
In February 2026 the board began exploring options, including selling the whole company. No deal is assured.
They plan to sell their India sales business and took $522 million in charges and write-downs to prepare it.
Risks they name: a key product (Rynaxypyr) losing patent protection, cheaper generic rivals, and cost cuts falling short.
Headlines report the stock falling, including a 13% drop and an analyst downgrade from KeyBanc.
A law firm says it is looking into an investigation on behalf of FMC investors.
Company director Luc Tack bought $14,078 of FMC stock.

takeaways: Sales and profits fell hard this quarter, partly from the company's own price cuts and partly from weaker demand.
Cash from operations improved versus last year, but the company expects more cash to go out than come in for the full year.
The company says the fixes take about three quarters and hopes for better results in 2027, but that is only its own forecast.

earnings.headline: Sales grew 6% and profit grew faster, while GoDaddy's AI website tool Airo picked up speed.
points: Revenue (sales) was $1.3 billion, up 6%. Software and payments grew 9%, but the domain side grew only 4%.
Net income (profit after all costs) was $261.8 million, up 24%. Free cash flow (cash left over) was $480.8 million.
Their forecast: 2026 sales near the top of $5.215 billion to $5.255 billion, and about $1.8 billion of free cash flow.
Airo bookings run rate passed $100 million, up from $50 million. But customers grew only 40 thousand, to 20.5 million.
They make money selling domain names (web addresses), websites, hosting, email and payment tools to small businesses.
2025 sales were $4,951.1 million, up 8.3%. About 85% of customers stay with them each year.
In 2025 they cut costs, like lower rent and moving to cloud servers, which made them more profitable.
Risks they name: AI changing how people build websites, tough competition, their debt, outages and cyberattacks.
Some headlines praise strong cash flow but warn of balance sheet risks, meaning the company carries a lot of debt.
The CFO says AI gives room to manage costs as Airo grows. Executives will speak at investor events in December.

takeaways: GoDaddy is growing slowly but steadily, and its profits are growing faster than its sales.
Its AI tool Airo is growing fast, but the older domain business is growing slowly and customer growth is small.
It owes a lot: total debt was $3.8 billion vs $1.1 billion cash, and it spent $1.4 billion buying back its own shares.

earnings.headline: Sales of Geron's one drug grew and the company made a small profit, but a big trial in a second blood cancer was stopped.
points: Sales (revenue) of RYTELO were $60.1 million this quarter, up from $47.2 million in the same quarter a year earlier.
They made a small profit of $1.4 million, after losing $18.4 million in the same quarter of 2025.
Their own forecast (guidance): 2026 RYTELO sales at the mid-to-high end of $220 million to $240 million; spending forecast cut.
Bad news: a late-stage trial of the drug in myelofibrosis, another blood cancer, was stopped because it was unlikely to work.
They make money selling RYTELO, a drug for a blood cancer called lower-risk MDS, sold in the U.S. since June 2024.
Europe approved the drug in March 2025, but the company says its sales outside the U.S. so far have been minimal.
Biggest risk they name: the company depends almost entirely on this one drug selling well.
Other named risks: rival drugs, getting insurers to pay, making enough supply, and keeping up with debt and royalty deals.
Insiders: the legal chief bought 12,000 shares at $0.94 each; three new hires got options on 150,000 shares at $1 each.
A law firm says it is looking into Geron over claimed problems with RYTELO's sales team.
Other headlines cover the planned Germany launch and RYTELO's growing sales.

takeaways: Geron's only drug is selling more, and the company turned a small profit this quarter.
A key trial in a second blood cancer was stopped, so the company's future rests heavily on RYTELO alone.
Cash rose to $339.4 million from $326.9 million; spending is down and Germany sales are expected by year end.

earnings.headline: Gilead's sales grew 13% to $8.3 billion, but profit per share fell to $1.94 from $2.43 a year ago.
points: Sales rose 13% to $8.3 billion. HIV drugs grew 18% to $6.2 billion, but COVID drug Veklury fell 69% to $86 million.
Profit per share fell to $1.94 from $2.43, from investment losses and higher costs. Their adjusted figure rose to $2.55.
They raised their full-year sales forecast (guidance) to 31,000-31,300 million dollars, but now expect a bigger loss per share.
Cash fell to $6.4 billion from $10.6 billion, mostly from buying companies. A Medicare price cap hits Biktarvy sales from January 1, 2028.
Gilead makes and sells medicines for HIV, liver disease, COVID-19 and cancer, in more than 35 countries.
In 2025, sales (revenue) grew 2% to $29.4 billion. Profit jumped to $8.5 billion from $480 million in 2024.
Setbacks: a cancer study (ASCENT-07) missed its main goal, another (STAR-221) was stopped, and the FDA paused two HIV drug trials.
Cheaper copies (generics) of Biktarvy, their biggest drug, can launch in the U.S. no earlier than April 1, 2036.
Headlines say the stock hit a new all-time high, and writers debate whether it is now priced too high.
An executive, Mercier, sold 28,000 shares for $4.78M under a trading plan set up in advance.

takeaways: HIV medicines are the engine: they make up most of Gilead's sales and grew fast this quarter.
Gilead spent heavily buying other companies, so its cash dropped and it expects a loss for the full year.
Biktarvy is a key drug to watch: a Medicare price cap starts in 2028 and cheaper copies can arrive in 2036.

earnings.headline: GM's sales and profit rose this quarter, but its overseas business, car-loan arm and China results earned less.
points: Revenue (sales) was $50.0 billion, up 2.9% from a year ago.
Net income (profit after all costs) was $3.3 billion, up from $1,327 million a year ago.
Weaker spots: international profit fell 87.7% to $28 million, and the car-loan arm (GM Financial) earned 16.9% less.
Their own forecast for 2026 profit is now $8.9 billion to $9.5 billion, below January's $10.3 billion to $11.7 billion.
GM makes money selling Chevrolet, GMC, Buick and Cadillac vehicles; big pickups and SUVs earn the most.
Tariffs (import taxes) cut 2025 profit by $3.1 billion; GM expects a $3.0 billion to $4.0 billion hit in 2026.
Electric car demand slowed after U.S. tax credits ended, so GM cut EV plans and took $7.9 billion in charges in 2025.
Risks they name: recalls, lawsuits, changing emissions rules, and currency swings in Canada, China and Korea.
GM moved its stock listing from the New York Stock Exchange to the Nasdaq.
Reuters, citing the WSJ, says GM hired a search firm to find a successor to CEO Mary Barra.

takeaways: GM earned more this quarter, mostly from North America, while its overseas and car-loan businesses earned less.
GM keeps repurchasing its own shares: 849 million now vs 904 million at the end of 2025, with $20.0 billion more approved.
Import taxes and slower EV demand are real costs, and GM's own 2026 profit forecast is lower than it was in January.

earnings.headline: Sales grew 4.2%, but reported profit was flat and the company trimmed the top of its own yearly forecast.
points: Sales (money from customers) rose 4.2% to $6.5 billion, up from $6.3 billion a year ago.
Profit was $224 million vs $226 million. Leaving out split and cleanup costs, profit per share rose to $2.07 from $1.98.
Their own forecast for 2026 profit per share narrowed to $7.50 to $7.75, cutting the top from $8.00.
Factory-parts profit grew 11.2%, but North America car-parts profit fell 2.9%.
They sell replacement car parts (NAPA) and factory parts. 2025 sales were $24.3 billion, about 74% from North America.
Sales grew 3.5% in 2025, mostly from taking over other businesses. Sales at existing locations grew only 0.9%.
Bad hits: a $151 million charge after supplier First Brands went bankrupt, and $103 million more set aside for asbestos claims.
Risks they name: weak shoppers, high interest rates, tariffs, and a planned split into two companies that may not go to plan.
The company kept its quarterly dividend (cash paid to owners) at $1.0625 a share, payable Jan. 5, 2027.
Several articles discuss it as a long-time dividend payer; research firm Stifel started covering it with a 'hold' rating.

takeaways: The business is still growing, mainly thanks to factory parts, while North America car parts earned less.
The company now expects a bit less profit this year than the best case it gave before.
A big change is coming: it plans to split into two separate companies in early 2027.

earnings.headline: Sales grew 11.3% to $324.4 million, but the company posted a $4.8 million loss after a profit a year ago.
points: Revenue (sales) was $324.4 million, up 11.3% from a year ago, helped most by Minnesota starting adult-use sales.
Net loss (they lost money) of $4.8 million, vs. a $23.3 million profit last year that included a one-time gain from a sale.
Costs rose: profit after product costs fell to 45.2% of sales from 49.4%, and running costs climbed to $121.7 million.
No sales forecast was given. They plan adult-use sales in Virginia from July 2027 and are working toward entering Texas.
They make and sell cannabis products under brands like RYTHM and Dogwalkers, and run their own RISE Dispensaries stores.
They operate in 14 U.S. markets, including Illinois, Florida, New York, Pennsylvania and Minnesota.
In February 2026 they borrowed more on their bank loan, which has a floating interest rate (it can go up or down).
Biggest risks they name: cannabis is still illegal under federal law, heavy competition, limited banking, and harsh tax rules.
Many headlines focus on the quarterly loss, which ended the company's run of profitable quarters.
Some ask whether sales at older stores are truly growing again after the federal rule change on medical cannabis.
Others cover the company's Florida store openings and a possibly friendlier political climate for cannabis.

takeaways: Sales are growing and older stores sold 3.0% more, but the company lost money this quarter as costs and fees rose.
They hold $316.0 million in cash against $277.3 million in total debt, so cash is larger than what they owe.
Federal rules are shifting: medical cannabis moved to Schedule III, cutting their tax bill, but much is still uncertain.

earnings.headline: Sales grew 21% to $286.3 million, but losses got bigger and cash from the business turned negative.
points: Sales (revenue) were $286.3 million, up 21% from a year ago. Big customers (over $100,000 a year) grew 17%.
Bad side: net loss grew to $36.8 million from $9.2 million. Adjusted profit, which skips some costs, was $42.1 million.
Cash from day-to-day business fell to $(3.1) million from $49.4 million a year ago, so cash went out instead of in.
Their own forecast (guidance) for next quarter's sales is $281 - $283 million, a bit below this quarter's $286.3 million.
GitLab sells software that teams use to plan, build, test and secure code, mostly through 1 to 3 year subscriptions.
Yearly sales were $955.2 million in fiscal year 2026, up 26%, but the net loss grew to $56.0 million from $6.3 million.
Existing customers still spent more, but less so: net retention fell to 118% from 123%, and 130% the year before.
Risks they name: growth could slow, strong competition, AI changing their market, and higher cloud costs from AI tools.
A company director, Sytse Sijbrandij, sold $5.49M of GitLab stock.
One article notes the stock had a 53% five year fall; another says analysts are split on the company.

takeaways: Sales keep growing at a solid pace, and more big customers are signing on.
But by official accounting rules, losses got bigger and less cash came in this quarter.
Their own forecast puts next quarter's sales a little below this quarter's, so growth may be cooling.

earnings.headline: Sales held steady at $5.7 billion, but reported profit fell from last quarter while profit before one-time charges rose.
points: Sales (revenue) were $5.7 billion, flat versus last quarter. North America fell 5%, while international sales rose 3%.
Profit fell to $417 million ($0.50 a share) from $534 million, partly due to a $107 million charge for write-downs.
Their own 2027 forecast: sales up a mid-single-digit percent and profit margins of about 15%, assuming a flat North America.
Cash left after spending (free cash flow) was only $156 million, yet they bought back about $250 million of their own stock.
They sell drilling and well services to oil and gas producers, with over 46,000 workers in more than 70 countries.
In 2025, total sales fell 3%: North America sales were down 6% and international sales were down 2%.
They returned $1.6 billion to shareholders in 2025 and aim to return over 50% of free cash flow in 2026.
They warn their forecasts can be wrong and actual results may differ a lot from what they plan.
Halliburton is reportedly proposing a 50-well drilling program in Egypt to grow its business there.
One headline notes the stock is down 7.5% since the last earnings report.
Several headlines are analyst opinions about the stock. Those are outside views, not company facts.

takeaways: Sales stayed steady, but reported profit dropped compared with last quarter.
Work outside North America, especially in the Middle East, is growing, while U.S. fracking work shrank.
Management expects better results in 2027, but that is their own forecast and it could miss.

earnings.headline: Halozyme's sales and profit grew strongly this quarter, and it raised its own forecast for the full year 2026.
points: Sales rose 39% from a year ago to $493 million. Royalties (fees partners pay to use its tech) rose 44% to $341 million.
Net income (profit after all costs) was $247.0 million, up from $175.2 million in the same quarter of 2025.
They raised their own forecast (guidance): 2026 total sales of $1.860 to $1.925 billion, up from $1.835 to $1.910 billion.
Costs rose too: research spending hit $27.8 million vs $17.3 million, and legal fees from a patent fight pushed up overhead.
They license ENHANZE, a tech that lets drugs be given as a quick shot under the skin instead of an IV drip, and collect royalties.
They added new delivery tech, Hypercon and Surf Bio, to make drugs more concentrated so smaller shots can carry the same dose.
Biggest named risks: drug approvals failing or delayed, supply problems, safety issues or recalls, and their patents being challenged.
They warn their convertible notes (loans that can turn into shares) could shrink current owners' slice of the company.
A Dutch court blocked Merck's Keytruda Qlex in several European countries over a Halozyme patent; the fight is ongoing.
Morgan Stanley downgraded the stock, saying the price already looks high for the business (valuation).
A director, Matthew Posard, sold $482,146 in company stock.

takeaways: The business is growing fast because more partner drugs use its shot-under-the-skin tech, and it pays Halozyme fees on each sale.
Costs are rising too, from new acquisitions and a costly patent fight with Merck that is not over yet.
It depends on partners' drugs getting approved and selling well, and on its patents holding up; problems there would hurt sales.

earnings.headline: Hasbro's sales grew 15% this quarter, led by Magic: The Gathering cards, and it raised its own forecast for 2026.
points: Sales (revenue) rose 15% vs. last year. Magic: The Gathering topped $600 million in one quarter for the first time.
Operating profit was $517 million. About $55 million of that came from refunds of past tariffs (import taxes).
Raised its own forecast (guidance): 2026 sales now seen up 7-9%, up from 5-7% before.
Weak spots: digital and licensed gaming grew only 3%, and film/TV sales are down 13% so far this year.
Hasbro sells toys and games, and earns fees (royalties) by letting others use its brands in apps, clothes, TV and film.
2025 sales rose 13.7% to $4,701.3 million, but a $1,021.9 million write-down of past purchases led to a loss.
Big named risk: tariffs. It paid about $44.9 million in tariff costs in 2025 and says changes could hurt sales and profit.
A cost-cutting plan has saved almost $800 million so far, toward a $1.0 billion goal.
One headline says Hasbro stock rose 29% in a month.
Another looks at how Hasbro's push into digital games could change its story.
Most other headlines are about the wider market, like slump worries and Nvidia, not Hasbro itself.

takeaways: Magic cards drive most of the growth, and Hasbro itself warns it now leans more and more on that one brand.
Part of this quarter's profit came from tariff refunds, which may not happen again.
The company raised its forecast and declared a $0.70 per share dividend, but forecasts can still miss.

earnings.headline: Sales and patient visits grew this quarter, but profit fell as more patients came in without insurance.
points: Sales (revenue) rose 3.6 percent to $19.849 billion. Hospital admissions rose 2.7 percent and ER visits rose 5.1 percent.
Profit (net income) fell 3.9 percent to $1.579 billion. Profit per share still rose to $7.27. Outpatient surgeries fell 3.7 percent.
More uninsured patients, many who lost exchange coverage, cut pre-tax profit by about $400 million this quarter.
Their own forecast (guidance): the full year should land in the upper half of the range they gave on July 14, 2026.
They make money running hospitals, surgery centers and clinics: 190 hospitals in 19 states and England at the end of 2025.
Cash from day-to-day business grew to $12.636 billion in 2025, up from $10.514 billion in 2024.
They spent $10.067 billion buying back their own shares in 2025, while total debt rose to $46.492 billion.
Biggest risk they name: heavy debt, which could limit their choices and raise interest costs if rates go up.
Several headlines say the stock fell as more uninsured patients and payment worries weighed on it.
Other headlines look at long-term stock returns and analyst forecasts, not new business news.

takeaways: More patients are coming in and sales grew, but profit dipped as more people showed up without insurance.
Federal insurance policy changes are hurting them, though the company says it expects to end the year well.
Debt is large and rising: $50.493 billion at September 30, 2026, compared with $908 million in cash.

earnings.headline: Warrior sold much more coal thanks to its new Blue Creek mine, earned more, and declared a $2.00 per-share special dividend.
points: Sales (revenue) were $507.9 million. They sold 48% more coal, and the average price they got was up 6%.
Profit (net income) was $49.3 million. Adjusted EBITDA, a cash-profit measure, rose 76% to $124.0 million.
Worse: cost to mine each ton rose 4% to $104.98, and they kept 66% of the top coal price vs 83% a year earlier.
They kept their own forecast (guidance) for 2026: 13.0 - 14.0 million short tons of coal sold.
